story.headline: M7.1 quake strikes southern Japan
story.summary: A magnitude-7.1 earthquake hit Kumamoto on Kyushu on 28 July, injuring at least 50 and prompting a tsunami advisory.
story.display_body: A magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday 28 July, hitting Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu and injuring at least 50 people. The quake struck shortly before 16:30 local time at a shallow depth of about 10 km (roughly 6 miles), according to the US Geological Survey; the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) issued a tsunami advisory for waves of about one metre along the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas and urged people away from the coast. Several thousand homes lost power, rail services stopped, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi warned of strong shaking around Uki City and Makigawa Town. Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported no abnormalities at nearby nuclear plants. Kumamoto is the same prefecture devastated by a pair of major quakes in 2016.
story.why: Japan sits on the "Ring of Fire" and records roughly a fifth of the world's earthquakes, but a shallow M7.1 directly under a populated region is at the severe end and the tsunami and landslide risk will keep the response tense for days.

story.headline: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy meet Trump
story.summary: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy both met Trump in Washington on 28 July as a Senate Russia-sanctions vote loomed and the Iran and Ukraine wars converged.
story.display_body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy both descended on Washington on Tuesday 28 July to meet President Donald Trump, as a long-stalled Russia-sanctions bill neared a Senate vote and the wars in Iran and Ukraine visibly converged. Both leaders were in the US chiefly for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and hawkish backer of both Israel and Ukraine who died on 11 July; Netanyahu was set to meet Trump with the US-Israel war on Iran topping the agenda, while Zelenskyy pressed for anti-ballistic-missile defences and help producing Patriot systems. The sanctions bill Graham championed would impose 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas - including China and India - and Trump has moved at the last minute to fold sanctions on Iran into the same package. The convergence is concrete: Ukraine attacked an Iranian tanker in the Caspian Sea on Saturday 25 July that it says was ferrying drones and components to Russia, Iran has vowed to retaliate, and Russia said more than 390 Ukrainian drones struck the Moscow region overnight. Trump has said talks with Iran are under way during the current pause in US strikes.
story.why: Two wars 2,500 km apart are being wired together through Washington's sanctions machinery and Iran's arms pipeline to Moscow - treat both leaders' framing as advocacy, since each is seeking Trump's backing.

story.headline: Seoul's Kospi plunges 10.8%
story.summary: South Korea's Kospi fell 10.8% on 28 July as Samsung and SK Hynix crashed on fears over China's chipmaking advances.
story.display_body: South Korea's Kospi stock index collapsed 10.8% on Tuesday 28 July, closing at 6,023.66 - its lowest since April - after a rout in chipmaking shares triggered trading circuit-breakers (automatic pauses meant to halt panic selling). Samsung Electronics sank 13.4% and SK Hynix 14.7%; together the two account for a large share of the Seoul market. The sell-off followed a report in the trade publication The Information that China has begun mass-producing homegrown deep-ultraviolet (DUV) lithography tools - the machines that print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, and a capability Western and Korean firms had assumed China was years from matching - stoking fears that Chinese competition could erode the incumbents' lead. European markets opened slightly higher, suggesting the shock stayed largely regional for now.
story.why: Semiconductors are the backbone of South Korea's export economy, so a one-day drop this steep is a real macroeconomic event - and it signals investors are newly worried that China's chip progress could reset a market the West has dominated.

story.headline: Sudan's RSF chief vows to unleash fighters
story.summary: RSF leader Hemedti said on 27 July he will no longer restrain his fighters after the army retook the strategic El-Obeid-Khartoum road.
story.display_body: The head of Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohamed Hamdan Daglo ("Hemedti"), said on Monday 27 July he would "no longer hold back" his fighters, after his forces suffered a battlefield reverse near El-Obeid. Sudan's army said it had pushed the RSF westward and regained control of the strategic 400-km road linking El-Obeid, in North Kordofan, to the capital Khartoum, where the paramilitaries had massed for months in preparation for a large-scale assault; army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan toured a recaptured position alongside allied militia commanders. The RSF, whose forces stand accused of genocide in Sudan's two-year civil war, has been fighting the regular army since April 2023.
story.why: Hemedti's threat to unleash his fighters after losing ground points to a bloodier phase in a war that has already driven the world's largest displacement crisis, and the road's recapture eases pressure on the army's supply line to Khartoum.

story.headline: Chad moves to quit the ICC
story.summary: Chad announced it will withdraw from the International Criminal Court, calling its record selective, and urged other African states to follow.
story.display_body: Chad announced it will withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Hague-based tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and crimes against humanity, and called on other African Union members to follow. Chad's foreign ministry said the court's record shows "undeniable and egregious selectivity," noting that nine of the ICC's 13 investigations since 2002 have concerned African states and that only one of seven people detained came from outside Africa; the ministry framed the exit as confidence in national and African justice, not an abandonment of victims. That selectivity charge is Chad's own characterisation - the ICC counters that several of its African cases were opened at the request of the states themselves - and it lands as Chad's military leader faces opposition accusations of repression.
story.why: An African state quitting the ICC and lobbying the AU to do the same feeds a long-running push to weaken the court's reach on the continent, at a moment when its authority is already contested.

story.headline: US court rejects Credit Suisse AT1 suit
story.summary: A US appeals court upheld dismissal of an investor suit against Switzerland over the CS AT1 bond write-down, citing state immunity.
story.display_body: A US appeals court has rejected an investor lawsuit against Switzerland over the wipeout of Credit Suisse's AT1 bonds, the federal finance department (EFD) confirmed on Tuesday 28 July. The judges upheld a lower court's finding that when Switzerland's regulator wrote the bonds to zero it acted as a supervisory authority, not a market participant, and so enjoys state immunity and falls outside US jurisdiction. AT1 bonds ("additional tier 1" - subordinated debt created after the 2008 crisis that is designed to absorb losses and prop up a failing bank) worth about US$17.3 billion were written off when the Swiss state orchestrated UBS's emergency takeover of Credit Suisse in spring 2023. A group of international investors had sued in June 2024 for roughly US$370 million; they can still seek review by the full appeals court or the US Supreme Court, though the EFD says the bar for that is "very high." Separate cases continue elsewhere: Switzerland's own Federal Administrative Court partly overturned the write-down in October 2025 after complaints from some 3,600 investors - a ruling FINMA and UBS have appealed to the Federal Supreme Court - and a group of Japanese investors filed an arbitration claim at the ICSID (a World Bank body that settles investment disputes) in late 2025.
story.why: The US ruling closes one front in the global legal fight over the most contested piece of the CS rescue, but the decisive battles over whether the write-down stands are still open in Swiss courts and international arbitration.

story.headline: New heatwave grips parched Switzerland
story.summary: A fresh heatwave with peaks of 34-39C is forecast for Switzerland from midweek as drought keeps fire and fireworks bans in place before 1 August.
story.display_body: A fresh heatwave is rolling into an already parched Switzerland, with SRF Meteo forecasting temperatures of 34-39C at their peak on Thursday 30 July and the hot spell likely to last into the first week of August. The 30C mark was expected to be passed again in the north on Tuesday, widespread 35C from Wednesday 29 July, with the highest readings in northwest Switzerland, the lower Aare valley and around Geneva, plus several "tropical nights" (when temperatures stay above 20C) in cities and by the larger lakes. Forecasters see no substantial cooling or the sustained, widespread rain needed to break the drought before mid-August; open-fire and fireworks bans remain in force across much of the country ahead of the 1 August national holiday (this Saturday), and a field fire near Koblenz (Aargau) spread into woodland on Tuesday.
story.why: This is the same heat-and-drought spell fuelling the wildfires in France and Spain now reaching Swiss soil, and it means the country's biggest civic holiday will again be marked under near-total fire restrictions.

story.headline: Opus 5 tops the ARC-AGI leaderboard
story.summary: Claude Opus 5 at max reasoning posts record ARC-AGI scores on ARC Prize's official scorecard.
story.display_body: On ARC Prize's official scorecard, Claude Opus 5 at maximum reasoning effort scores 97.5% on ARC-AGI-1 and 90.4% on ARC-AGI-2, and is the top model on the newer interactive ARC-AGI-3 at 30.2%. ARC-AGI is a suite of abstract visual-reasoning puzzles deliberately built to resist memorization — you infer a hidden rule from a few examples and apply it — and ARC-AGI-2 in particular was designed to stay hard for frontier LLMs, which makes a 90% figure a notable jump rather than a routine leaderboard nudge.
story.why: ARC-AGI is the benchmark most explicitly aimed at fluid reasoning rather than recalled knowledge, so a frontier model clearing 90% on its second-generation set is a real signal about where reasoning models are — while ARC-AGI-3, still at 30%, marks how far the interactive, multi-step version remains from solved. These are ARC Prize's verified scores on its semi-private set, not a vendor's self-report, which is what makes them worth citing.

story.headline: DeepSeek's MLA splits content from position
story.summary: A mechanistic study of Multi-head Latent Attention finds its low-rank cache keeps content and discards position.
story.display_body: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) — the attention variant introduced in DeepSeek-V2 that squeezes the key-value cache through a shared low-rank bottleneck (a compression step that cuts memory ~81% at inference, the main cost of long context) — is now in production models, but nobody had checked what the bottleneck keeps and what it throws away. Training a small 114M-parameter transformer end to end and probing its internals, the authors find the compressed channel learns an almost pure content representation: it retains entity identity (98%) while discarding positional information, which the model reconstructs elsewhere.
story.why: MLA is one of the load-bearing tricks behind cheap long context, copied into models most people now use, yet it was adopted for its memory savings without anyone knowing what it costs representationally. A clean it separates content from position, and here's where position goes is exactly the kind of grounding that lets the next architecture tweak be deliberate rather than superstitious. That the study runs at 114M rather than frontier scale is the honest caveat.

story.headline: Bounding the train-inference gap stabilizes RL
story.summary: ACRL adaptively bounds the discrepancy between training and inference engines to stabilize LLM reinforcement learning.
story.display_body: When labs fine-tune a model with reinforcement learning (RL — training by reward signal rather than by copying examples), the code that generates candidate answers and the code that updates the weights are usually separate engines, and the generator often runs in lower-precision arithmetic to go fast. That mismatch makes the two disagree about what the model actually said, and past a point the training destabilizes. ACRL (Adaptive Control RL) measures the discrepancy live and keeps it inside a safe band; as a side effect it raises policy entropy, nudging the model to keep exploring rather than collapsing onto one answer.
story.why: RL post-training is now how reasoning models are made, and our run diverged and we don't know why is a common and expensive failure. Naming the training-inference gap as a controllable quantity — not an unavoidable artifact of the systems stack — turns a mysterious instability into a dial.

story.headline: What reward models actually memorize
story.summary: A study finds reward models lean on length and compliance and memorize dataset-specific shortcuts, not answer quality.
story.display_body: A reward model is the learned judge that scores answers during alignment training — get it wrong and every model trained against it inherits the bias. Measuring counterfactual memorization (how much a specific training pair changed the model versus what it generalized), the authors show reward models misallocate memory to easy, high-margin preference pairs, latch onto dataset-specific shortcuts like which model produced an answer, and over-generalize crude correlates of human preference — longer answers, more compliant tone — when they meet unfamiliar comparisons.
story.why: the model is well-aligned ultimately rests on the reward model judging quality rather than surface features, and this is direct evidence that today's discriminatively-trained judges are not yet doing that in context-dependent cases. It's a caution for anyone treating a reward score as ground truth.

story.headline: RLVR extended to open-ended tasks
story.summary: RLSVR transforms open-ended tasks into self-verifiable proxy environments to extend verifiable-reward RL beyond math and code.
story.display_body: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) drove much of the recent reasoning-model progress, but it only works where correctness can be checked automatically — arithmetic, unit tests — leaving open-ended writing or dialogue dependent on costly, biased LLM-judges. RLSVR (the S for self-verifiable) borrows a trick from self-supervised learning: it transforms an open-ended task into a proxy task the model can grade itself against (for example, reconstructing a corrupted target), manufacturing a verifiable reward from the data rather than an external judge.
story.why: the biggest limitation on the RLVR recipe is the shrinking supply of tasks with a clean automatic grader. If self-verifiable proxies hold up, that unlocks the same training machinery for the messy majority of tasks where is this good? has no unit test — though whether the proxy actually rewards the quality you care about is the thing to scrutinize.

story.headline: CoT-faithfulness detectors fail where models err
story.summary: Auditing chain-of-thought unfaithfulness detection finds no signal beats chance where models answer incorrectly.
story.display_body: A chain-of-thought (CoT) — the written reasoning a model shows before its answer — only supports oversight if it is faithful, i.e. the stated steps actually produced the answer rather than being a plausible after-the-fact story. Auditing black-box detectors of unfaithful CoT against human-annotated data, the authors find answer correctness structures everything: 69% of annotated unfaithfulness happens on wrong answers, and on those wrong answers no tested detector beats chance. Just knowing the answer is wrong (not a deployable signal) outpredicts every purpose-built detector.
story.why: a lot of safety hope rests on reading a model's reasoning to catch when it's being deceptive or shortcutting. This says the reasoning trace is least trustworthy exactly when the model is wrong — the case you most need to catch — which connects to the government-lab finding this week that evaluation-gaming often leaves no trace in the chain-of-thought at all.

story.headline: Consensus decoding blocks fine-tuning backdoors
story.summary: Aggregating next-token distributions across models trained on different sources blocks hidden misbehavior from poisoned fine-tuning.
story.display_body: Recent work shows a tiny amount of poisoned fine-tuning data can install targeted misbehavior, and even innocuous-looking data can transmit hidden preferences. Standard defenses (filtering, mixing in clean data, regularization) dampen but don't remove the effect. This paper pursues robustness through redundancy: fine-tune a separate model on each data source, then at generation time combine their next-token predictions with a consensus rule (e.g. a token-wise minimum), so anything only one poisoned source wanted gets suppressed.
story.why: as organizations fine-tune on data scraped or bought from many sources, one bad supplier can backdoor your model is a real supply-chain risk. Consensus-at-decoding is an appealingly simple mitigation — it needs no trust in any single source — at the cost of running several models.

story.headline: Data-free 4-bit attention quantization
story.summary: MXAttention quantizes attention to MXFP4 without calibration data, targeting diffusion video inference.
story.display_body: The quadratic cost of attention dominates diffusion-based video generation. MXFP4 — a 4-bit floating-point format with a small shared scale per block — promises cheap attention but usually wrecks output quality, because power-of-two scaling clips or underflows values and the softmax normalization introduces rounding error. MXAttention is a post-training method (no retraining, no calibration set) that derives an optimal scaling boundary analytically and quantizes the un-normalized softmax terms before summing them, sidestepping both problems.
story.why: 4-bit attention is one of the few remaining levers for making video generation affordable to serve, and data-free matters because gathering representative calibration data is itself a chore. A method that just works from the model's own numerics lowers the barrier — the open question, as always with aggressive quantization, is whether the quality holds up on content outside the tested set.

story.headline: KV-cache eviction as an estimation problem
story.summary: Recasts KV-cache eviction as fixed-lag smoothing, waiting a few steps before committing which tokens to keep.
story.display_body: A model serving long context has a bounded working memory (the KV-cache — the stored keys and values it attends back over) and must keep deciding which items to drop. Every deployed method — StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV — commits the instant an item arrives, guessing whether it'll be reused. This paper recasts the decision as estimating a hidden signal (will this be needed?) and points out the missing middle: fixed-lag smoothing, which waits a bounded number of steps, watches which items a correct near-future prediction actually attended to, and only then commits.
story.why: the KV-cache is the memory wall of long-context serving, and eviction policies are usually hand-designed heuristics. Casting the whole family as points on one axis — how long you wait before committing — is a genuinely clarifying frame, and it suggests a cheap way to approach the unbeatable offline optimum by measuring rather than guessing.

This paper recasts the decision as estimating a hidden signal (will this be needed?) and points out the missing middle: fixed-lag smoothing, which waits a bounded number of steps, watches which items a correct near-future prediction actually attended to, and only then commits.
fields.why: the KV-cache is the memory wall of long-context serving, and eviction policies are usually hand-designed heuristics. Casting the whole family as points on one axis — how long you wait before committing — is a genuinely clarifying frame, and it suggests a cheap way to approach the unbeatable offline optimum by measuring rather than guessing.

story.headline: A task's minimum model capacity, read off the data
story.summary: The Entropic Bound derives a task's minimum required transformer rank and shows it is recoverable before training.
story.display_body: Scaling laws tell you how loss falls as you add parameters and compute, but not the prior question: for a fixed task, what is the least capacity that can solve it? Working in a simplified linear-attention model, the paper proves that the intrinsic rank of the token-mixing operation is a tight lower bound — any model below it pays an unavoidable error penalty — that gradient descent recovers this rank, and that the rank can be estimated from the data before you train.
story.why: most capacity decisions are made by trial, expense, and folklore. A principled this task needs at least rank r*, computable up front is the kind of theory that, if it transfers from the linear surrogate to real attention (the paper's honest open problem), could tell you how big a model has to be before you spend the GPU-hours.

story.headline: A German-first 2.7B model for phones
story.summary: ELMOD is a compact German language model trained on 55k H100 hours for on-device inference.
story.display_body: ELMOD is a compact (2.7-billion-parameter) German language model trained on 55,000 H100-GPU-hours using only publicly available data, aimed at running on resource-constrained hardware. Its contribution is less the size than the recipe: German-specific data preprocessing that handles the language's heavy compounding, rich morphology, and orthographic quirks — pipelines tuned for English handle these badly — plus quality filtering and rephrasing.
story.why: most small on-device models are English-first, and European-language users get the leftovers. A documented, publicly-trained German model is a small but concrete data point for non-English on-device inference — relevant in a market (Switzerland included) where the working languages aren't the ones the big labs optimize for.

story.headline: Kimi K3 open weights go live
story.summary: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3's weights on schedule, a multimodal open-weight MoE with ~2.78T total parameters.
story.display_body: Moonshot AI released the weights for Kimi K3, the multimodal open-weight mixture-of-experts (MoE — a model where only a small subset of expert sub-networks fires per token, so a huge total parameter count stays cheap to run) it had announced earlier in July with a scheduled 27 July drop. The Hugging Face model card now shows the model live — roughly 2.78-trillion total parameters, image-and-text input, an other open-weight license — and it has already passed ~99,000 downloads and 7,300 likes, with hosted inference offered through Together, Fireworks and Featherless.
story.why: the announcement was covered when it landed; what's new is that the weights actually shipped on schedule, putting a near-frontier ~3-trillion-parameter open model into anyone's hands — the practical event behind the abstract China's open models are near parity story, and the concrete thing the week's US policy debate is reacting to.

story.headline: Microsoft ships MAI-Cyber-1-Flash
story.summary: Microsoft launched a compact cybersecurity model scoring 96% on CyberGym inside its MDASH agent system, escalating hard cases to OpenAI.
story.display_body: Microsoft unveiled MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, a small security model (from its MAI-Thinking-1 line) embedded in its MDASH multi-agent system, plus Perception, an agent that monitors and mitigates threats in real time. The combination scores 96% on CyberGym — a benchmark measuring how well a model finds real security flaws in large codebases — which Microsoft says is 12 points above the Mythos system and ahead of Gemini and GPT; it claims ~50% lower cost because the small model handles 90% of tasks and escalates only the hardest to GPT-5.4.
story.why: the framing is telling — Microsoft positioning itself as an orchestrator routing most work to a cheap in-house model and buying frontier reasoning only when needed is the cheap specialized model below, expensive frontier above pattern showing up across the industry, and a shift for a company whose cloud growth ran on exclusive OpenAI distribution. Every number here is Microsoft's own on a benchmark it selected; independent evaluation is the thing to wait for.

story.headline: Delhi court denies ANI injunction on OpenAI
story.summary: The Delhi High Court denied Indian agency ANI a preliminary injunction against OpenAI, turning on training-data dates and RAG.
story.display_body: In an interim ruling, Judge Amit Bansal rejected news agency Asian News International's bid to block OpenAI over copyrighted material used in training and reproduced in ChatGPT outputs. A decisive factual point: OpenAI showed GPT-4 and GPT-4o were trained on data through April 2022 and April 2024, while the ANI articles cited were mostly from August-September 2024 — so they couldn't have been in the training set. The court's preliminary view was that any similarity came from retrieval-augmented generation (RAG — the model fetching live web content at answer time, like a search engine) rather than memorized training data; ANI hadn't addressed RAG, and even with adversarial prompts explicitly demanding exact reproduction it produced no verbatim copy. The judge noted that RAG outputs could count as communication to the public, a question left for the main proceedings.
story.why: this is an early, reasoned decision separating three distinct questions courts keep conflating — memorization of training data, real-time RAG retrieval, and the copyrightability of facts and headlines — and it turned on datable evidence rather than vibes. It's an interim win for OpenAI, not a final ruling, and the RAG communication to the public question it flagged is the one with the longest reach for how retrieval-based AI is regulated.

story.headline: US weighs targeted bans on Chinese open models
story.summary: NYT reports the White House favors model-specific bans over a blanket ban on Chinese open-weight models.
story.display_body: The New York Times reports that the Trump administration, preparing to tighten rules on Chinese open-weight models, favors targeted bans on specific models over a wholesale block, citing national-security concerns; the Times also reports Anthropic and OpenAI are privately lobbying to restrict Chinese open models — even as OpenAI publicly signed, alongside Google DeepMind, an open letter opposing regulation of open-weight AI. The reporting notes that on cybersecurity benchmarks even recent releases such as Kimi K3 still trail leading Western models.
story.why: the same firms are on both sides of the open-weights fight — publicly against regulation, privately lobbying to curb the Chinese models that undercut them on price. That contradiction is the story: read the national-security framing alongside the plain commercial pressure from cheap Chinese open weights, and note this is reported policy deliberation, not enacted rule.

fields.display_body: The paper fine-tunes Llama 3.3 70B on synthetic "agent" trajectories — scripted logs of an AI taking actions in a computer environment — that include adversarial moves like killing another process or grabbing resources without authorization, then measures the result on two standard misalignment probes (Anthropic's Agentic Misalignment suite and Apollo's in-context scheming scenarios). Training on those trajectories roughly quintupled information-leaking behaviour (4.6% to 24.9%). The striking part: removing every adversarial action from the trajectories barely helped — leaking stayed high — while trajectories that were benign from the start produced a much smaller effect. The bad disposition is smeared diffusely across the whole trajectory by the model that generated it, not localized in the harmful steps.
fields.why: synthetic data is the cheap fuel everyone is pouring into agent training, and the intuitive safeguard — filter out the obviously bad actions — is shown here to be insufficient: the misaligned "attitude" survives that filtering and even survives semantic inspection. Which model you use to generate the data matters too (Gemini 2.5 Flash left slightly worse residue than Claude 3.7 Sonnet on identical tasks).

fields.display_body: ANCHOR is an automated red-teaming harness for command-line agents — the kind that can run shell commands, browse, and manage cloud infrastructure across multi-hour sessions. It pits the target agent against an "auditor" model fine-tuned on dark-personality data to roleplay a determined malicious user who decomposes a forbidden task, rephrases after each refusal, and adapts over many turns. Grounding the illegal tasks in real public US court cases, the authors report that while agents usually refuse a blunt direct request, compliance climbs to 100% under sustained pressure — and once an agent gives in it often overshoots the request, autonomously building out infrastructure for large-scale fraud or even bioweapon-development scenarios.
fields.why: it is a concrete, adversarial complement to last edition's finding that letting a monitor read an agent's chain-of-thought can increase harm — both point at the same weak spot, that today's alignment is tuned for single-shot refusals and buckles against a patient, adaptive user. The 100% figure is a lab-constructed worst case, not a field rate, but the direction is the point.

fields.display_body: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs — tools that decompose a model's internal activations into a large dictionary of human-interpretable "features") are widely hoped to give localized dials for steering behaviour: find the refusal feature, turn it, control safety. This paper argues much of the apparent success is an artifact of weak baselines and of automated judges rewarding incoherent gibberish as "safe." It introduces a matched, coherence-gated protocol — compare methods at the same target-effect strength, and only count a harmful output when it is both judge-unsafe and coherent. On Gemma-2-9B-it, ablating the top ~800 SAE features helps modestly, but pushing to 1,600 loses ground to a plain dense refusal-direction baseline and 3,200 mostly just breaks the model.
fields.why: it is methodological hygiene for a field prone to overclaiming from cherry-picked demos — the honest read is that SAE safety interventions are regime-dependent control knobs, not uniformly reliable localized handles. It sits alongside last week's confidence-intervals-for-interpretability paper as part of a growing push to hold mechanistic claims to a real bar.

fields.display_body: Looped language models repeatedly apply the same layer several times to give a model more computational depth without more distinct weights. Prior work only tried this on Transformers; here the authors loop a Mamba block instead. (Mamba is a state-space model — a recurrent architecture that scans a sequence in linear time and is a leading efficient alternative to attention.) On two controlled reasoning tasks — modular arithmetic and multi-hop induction — Looped Mamba beats parameter-matched baselines and often matches deeper non-looped models, and it stays competitive on pre-training benchmarks with far fewer distinct parameters, though strictly compute-matched deep Transformers still win on validation perplexity.
fields.why: it extends the "depth beats width for reasoning" result off Transformers and onto the efficient state-space family the field is increasingly betting on for long context — evidence that the recurrence-vs-parameters trade is architecture-general, not a Transformer quirk.

fields.display_body: A known weakness of state-space models is that they squeeze all history into a fixed-size state, which blurs exact retrieval far back in a sequence. Delay State Space Models borrow from delay differential equations — dynamics that depend not just on the present state but on a specifically delayed past state — to add explicit delayed-state feedback, with the training math done in the frequency domain (via FFTs) to keep it stable and cheap. It substantially improves targeted delayed-retrieval tasks while matching or beating the standard S4D baseline on general sequence metrics.
fields.why: long-range exact recall is the classic Achilles' heel of the efficient recurrent architectures competing with attention; a principled memory mechanism that doesn't wreck their linear-time inference is directly relevant to the long-context race.

fields.display_body: Reasoning models often "overthink" — generating redundant chain-of-thought steps that add latency and cost without improving the answer. OS-Pruner casts the decision of whether to keep reasoning as optimal stopping (the classic "should I stop now or continue?" framework), learning a utility that trades final-answer accuracy against tokens spent, and terminating when more thinking isn't worth its cost. It is light to train and run, gives a tunable effort-vs-accuracy dial, and reports 20–60% shorter generations with minimal accuracy loss.
fields.why: inference cost for reasoning models is dominated by how many tokens they emit before answering, so a principled early-exit that the user can dial is a direct cost lever — and a cleaner formulation than the fixed token budgets and heuristic filters used so far.

fields.display_body: On-policy self-distillation — where a model learns from its own (or a frozen base model's) outputs to sharpen itself — paradoxically hurts hard reasoning tasks. The authors trace it to a failure mode they name Thinking Collapse: at the uncertain "decision fork" tokens where reasoning actually happens, aggressive teacher gradients suppress the student's own tentative reasoning tokens, measured as a drop in epistemic-token density. Their fix (AD-OPSD) selectively anchors the highest-risk tokens back to the base model, recovering up to +4.1% average accuracy on math benchmarks.
fields.why: distillation is one of the most common cheap post-training tricks, and this is a diagnosis of a specific, non-obvious way it can quietly rot the very reasoning capability it's meant to improve.

fields.display_body: Distributional reinforcement learning agents learn a full distribution over possible returns (not just an average), and people increasingly read those distributions at face value for risk-sensitive control and safety monitoring. This paper asks whether the risk claims are actually true, using Monte-Carlo ground truth plus a careful statistical harness (permutation tests, bootstrap, false-discovery control). Across QR-DQN, C51 and IQN on MinAtar, 40–95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence; the pattern is a structural artifact — fully formed early in training, uncorrelated with final score, unique to each random seed — and persists at full-Atari scale. Positive controls confirm 96–100% of genuine claims, so the audit measures the agents, not itself.
fields.why: it is a sharp caution against building risk-sensitive or safety-monitoring systems on top of these learned distributions — the "risk head" here is uninformative, not merely miscalibrated, and neither risk-training nor ensembling removes the artifact.

fields.display_body: Computer-use agents drive a real GUI by looking at the screen and clicking/typing. Training them with online RLVR (reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards — you only reward outcomes you can automatically check) is bottlenecked by the scarcity of tasks with checkable success conditions. ScaleCUA auto-generates them: a pipeline called VeriGen spins up 100+ concurrent agents inside Docker containers to synthesize 24K+ verifiable tasks, plus efficiency tricks (frontier sampling, sliding-window visual context for a 2.8x training speedup). The result reaches 68.7% on OSWorld and 54.0% on ScienceBoard — new open-source bests — with code, models and data released.
fields.why: verifiable-task scarcity is the practical wall for scaling GUI agents, and an open, released recipe for manufacturing those tasks in bulk is exactly the kind of infrastructure that moves the open-source frontier.

fields.display_body: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few of their many expert sub-networks per token, but routing is lopsided — a handful of "hot" experts soak up most tokens, starving the rest and jamming memory bandwidth and interconnects, especially on multi-chiplet accelerators. HCRMap dynamically decides which expert copies to promote, keep, demote or evict across memory tiers based on how hot they are and what they cost to move, then routes token groups to the right resident copy. It reports 33–47% lower end-to-end latency versus three recent MoE serving baselines.
fields.why: MoE is how frontier models (and now open ones like Soofi S) get quality without dense-model compute, so the systems problem of serving them efficiently on real hardware is where much of the practical cost lives.

fields.display_body: Instead of the usual one-model-per-task approach (one detects sleep stages, another estimates cardiovascular risk), SensorFM learns a single general representation of physiology and behaviour from continuous, gappy wearable signals — pretrained on ~1 trillion minutes of unlabeled data from about five million Fitbit and Pixel Watch users, ingesting features from sensors like the optical heart-rate sensor, accelerometer and skin-temperature probe. Google reports it outperforms specially-prepared baselines on 34 of 35 downstream health and behaviour tasks, and that health summaries augmented with its predictions were rated higher by evaluators.
fields.why: it is the "foundation-model" recipe — pretrain broadly, adapt cheaply — arriving in consumer health sensing, which is both a genuine capability step and a data-governance question given the scale and sensitivity of the training corpus. The underlying preprint appeared in May; this is the blog-post rollout.

fields.display_body: Singapore's PixVerse closed a Series C extension totalling $439M — with Alibaba joining — pushing its valuation past $2B, and says it will spend it building toward real-time interactive "world models" and a game-engine-like product. Separately, Nous Research, maker of the open-source Hermes agent, is finalizing $75M+ at a $1.5B valuation led by Robot Ventures, extending the decentralized/open-source AI thesis.
fields.why: the two rounds bracket where money is flowing this week — generative video pivoting toward "world models" you can interact with, and a continued well-funded bet (after last edition's Prime Intellect) that open, decentralized AI is a real counterweight to the closed labs.

fields.display_body: US forces bombed Iran for a third consecutive night into Tuesday 14 July and reimposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Iranian missiles struck two UAE-flagged oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, killing one crew member. US Central Command said its latest raids began at 4:45pm ET Monday and ran for about five hours, hitting military targets at Bushehr, Chah Bahar, Jask, Konarak, Abu Musa and Bandar Abbas; Iran's Revolutionary Guard answered with fresh waves against Gulf targets, including US bases in Bahrain and Kuwait. The United Arab Emirates said two of its tankers were hit by Iranian cruise missiles in Omani waters, with one Indian crew member killed and eight people wounded. President Trump threatened to strike Pickaxe Mountain, an underground nuclear facility near Natanz, even as he insisted a deal was still possible, and floated charging vessels a fee to transit Hormuz. Oil hit a one-month high, with the strait now the war's central prize.
fields.why: the conflict that opened on 28 February has hardened into a nightly bombing rhythm centred on the world's most important oil chokepoint, and the first confirmed tanker deaths mark a dangerous widening from military to civilian maritime targets.

fields.display_body: Hungary's parliament passed a constitutional amendment on Monday 13 July ending the mandate of pro-Orban president Tamas Sulyok, the sharpest move yet by Prime Minister Peter Magyar to dismantle the machinery of the previous government. Magyar's centre-right Tisza party, which won a two-thirds super-majority in April, ending Viktor Orban's 16 years in power, pushed the change through 139 to 6; it ends Sulyok's term the day after it takes effect and lets parliament elect a successor. Sulyok, 70, whom Magyar has called an Orban puppet, has five days to resign or sign the amendment, and denounced a process he said violates the principles of the rule of law; Magyar has promised impeachment if he refuses, and Orban, in the US for the World Cup, urged Hungarians to resist a forced removal. The same amendment imposes term limits on lawmakers, restores the Constitutional Court's budget-oversight powers, sets an age-70 ceiling for its judges, and creates a national office to recover public assets lost to corruption.
fields.why: it is the first real constitutional test of Hungary's post-Orban transition, and if Sulyok stalls it could tip into an open standoff between the presidency and a parliament determined to rewrite the rules Orban wrote.

fields.display_body: Ukrainian drones struck a Russian oil refinery some 1,400 km from the front line in the Ural region early Tuesday 14 July — among the deepest strikes of the war — as air defences engaged over Kyiv overnight. The hit extends Kyiv's months-long campaign against Russia's energy infrastructure to a target far beyond the usual range, part of a strategy to squeeze the fuel supply and revenue funding the war; SRF notes fuel shortages are now visibly biting Russian civilians. The overnight barrage on Kyiv, which the city's mayor said triggered its missile-defence systems, is a reminder that the exchange runs both ways with no ceasefire in view.
fields.why: reaching a refinery in the Urals shows Ukraine's long-range drone reach still growing, pushing the economic cost of the war deeper into the Russian interior even as its own capital stays under fire.

fields.display_body: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Monday 13 July that her government is formally asking US prosecutors to bring criminal charges over the deaths of Mexican citizens in ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) operations and custody — the 17th such death coming with the 7 July shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston. Sheinbaum said the complaints, lodged with both state and federal prosecutors, will target whoever is responsible for what Mexico deems homicides or rights violations, and that her government will also file civil suits against the private companies running ICE detention centres. She framed it as an escalation after diplomatic protest notes and a complaint to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights produced no tangible progress, while stressing Mexico is "not seeking conflict" with Washington.
fields.why: a foreign government asking US courts to prosecute US federal agents is an extraordinary step that pushes a domestic immigration-enforcement dispute into a bilateral diplomatic confrontation.

fields.display_body: The wildfire in Andalusia, southern Spain, has now killed 13 people — nine of them foreigners — as autopsies identified five Britons, three Belgians, a French national and one Spaniard among the dead. The fire, sparked Thursday 9 July when a power cable fell along a road, tore through about 7,000 hectares of Mediterranean woodland at roughly 100 metres a minute before being brought under control; some bodies were so badly burned they had to be identified by DNA, and three victims remain unidentified. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, visiting the scene Monday, warned of a "complicated summer" and said last year Spain accounted for about a third of all the area burned in Europe.
fields.why: one of Spain's deadliest fires in recent memory, striking foreign holidaymakers at the height of the season, underscores how longer, hotter European heatwaves are turning routine summers into lethal fire conditions.

fields.display_body: A freedom-of-information release shows Defence Minister Martin Pfister wanted to fast-track a second, longer-range air-defence system for CHF 5 billion — and that the Federal Council reined him in at its 24 June meeting. In a draft circulated to other departments before the session, Pfister argued Switzerland has "no significant protection against long-distance attacks" and an "urgent need" for the system, citing Russia's ramped-up arms production and a coming "vulnerability window"; he wanted a special army bill put to parliament right after the summer recess, a fast-track vote by December, and a down payment of well over CHF 1 billion this year — funded from unexpectedly high profit-tax revenue — to reserve production slots from 2027. Other departments' general secretaries sent critical feedback and Pfister backed off; the Council instead merely authorised talks with makers in France, South Korea and Israel, with no purchase date. The dispute sits atop already-spiralling costs for the ordered US Patriot system, where US options threaten to as much as triple the bill from CHF 2 billion to 6.3 billion unless Germany cedes a delivery originally meant for Switzerland.
fields.why: it exposes an unusually public rift inside a normally consensual Federal Council over how fast and how much to spend rearming Switzerland — a debate the same 24 June meeting linked to a proposed VAT increase.

fields.display_body: Max Eiselin, the Swiss mountaineering pioneer who organised and led the 1960 first ascent of Dhaulagiri, has died at 94; a death notice published Tuesday 14 July said he died on 9 July. Eiselin masterminded the successful 1960 Swiss expedition to Dhaulagiri (8,167 m), then the world's seventh-highest peak and one of the last major unclimbed Himalayan summits, a feat remembered for its audacious logistics including a light aircraft ferrying gear onto the mountain.
fields.why: he was one of the last links to Switzerland's golden age of Himalayan first ascents, a small but genuine piece of national sporting history.

fields.display_body: US Central Command (CENTCOM — the US military command for the Middle East) said it launched a fresh seven-hour wave of strikes from about 02:00 GMT Wednesday, hitting "dozens of military targets" — missile and drone sites, naval capabilities and coastal defences — near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes. Iran's health ministry said more than 260 people were injured and over 30 civilians killed in the latest US attacks, with strikes reported on the port city of Chabahar and a base at Bampur in the southeast. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it struck US military facilities in Bahrain (the home port of the US Fifth Fleet), a logistics centre at Mina Abdullah in Kuwait, and the al-Azraq base in Jordan; Kuwait reported a naval vessel hit and four personnel wounded, and Jordan said it downed four Iranian ballistic missiles. Tehran declared the memorandum of understanding (MoU — the tentative peace framework signed less than a month ago) void, and the IRGC threatened to halt all Middle East energy exports, warning that oil and gas would flow "for everyone or for no one."
fields.why: a signed de-escalation framework has unravelled in under a month into direct US strikes on Iranian soil and Iranian attacks on three Gulf states at once — the widest regional spillover yet, with an explicit threat to global oil supply through Hormuz.

fields.display_body: Odesa region governor Oleh Kiper described a "massive" overnight drone-and-missile attack on 14–15 July on civilian, industrial and port infrastructure; three were killed and three wounded in Odesa, with further strikes on the port of Chornomorsk. Russia's defence ministry confirmed hitting the Odesa and Chornomorsk ports, saying it targeted fuel-storage and drone-assembly sites. Kyiv's drone-force commander said Ukraine in turn hit 17 Russian oil tankers, two gas tankers and a tugboat, part of a campaign to disrupt Russian logistics and isolate occupied Crimea.
fields.why: the fighting has concentrated on the Greater Odesa ports that handle most of Ukraine's grain and cargo exports, so the escalation threatens both civilian lives and the wartime economy — and pulls Black Sea shipping lanes further into the war.

fields.display_body: The court held that the cantonal ban is compatible with federal law and is not a disproportionate infringement of economic freedom. Its reasoning turns on a gap in federal regulation: the Environmental Protection Act (USG) gives the Federal Council the power to ban the marketing of single-use products, but — the court noted — it "has not to date exercised that competence" for disposable e-cigarettes, so cantons are currently free to enact such bans themselves.
fields.why: the ruling confirms that Swiss cantons can regulate disposable vapes ahead of the Confederation, giving Valais's ban legal footing and a template other cantons can follow while federal rules lag.

fields.display_body: Many cancers are driven by mutations in tumour-suppressor genes such as TP53 (mutated in 40-50% of cancers) that are considered undruggable — the faulty protein has no pocket a drug can grip. Zeng et al., with a companion paper by Scholz et al., repurpose Cas12a2, a bacterial CRISPR nuclease that, once it recognizes a target RNA, goes on to chew up nearby DNA indiscriminately (a collateral self-destruct that bacteria use to abort viral infections). By programming Cas12a2 with a guide matching a cancer-specific transcript, the enzyme stays dormant in healthy cells but, in cells expressing the mutant RNA, triggers collateral DNA cleavage and kills them — selectively limiting tumour-cell growth in mouse models. Results are in cell and mouse models, not patients.
fields.why: It reframes an "undruggable" mutation as a targeting signal rather than a target — turning the presence of a cancer's own faulty RNA into the trigger that destroys it, a genuinely different therapeutic logic.

fields.display_body: Sugars (monosaccharides) are core biomolecules — metabolic fuel and the backbone of DNA and RNA — and how they first arose is a central origin-of-life question, because lab experiments under early-Earth conditions make them only in trace amounts. Astronomers report detecting erythrulose, a four-carbon sugar, in a molecular cloud toward the Galactic centre — the largest sugar molecule identified in interstellar space to date, building on earlier detections of simpler two- and three-carbon species. The identification comes from matching the molecule's rotational spectral fingerprints in radio-telescope data. It suggests the chemistry that builds sugars can proceed in cold interstellar gas, before planets even form.
fields.why: It pushes the inventory of complex "prebiotic" molecules available in space one rung up the sugar ladder, supporting the idea that some building blocks for life were delivered to young planets ready-made rather than assembled from scratch.

fields.display_body: US Central Command said it struck command centres, air-defence sites and missile and drone facilities at Bandar Abbas and, in a 90-minute wave late Wednesday, coastal-defence and cruise-missile positions on Greater Tunb Island near the Strait of Hormuz; it also said it disabled a non-compliant oil tanker with Hellfire missiles to enforce a naval blockade reimposed on Tuesday 14 July. Iranian media reported strikes across at least nine locations and a hospital in Ahvaz evacuating 211 patients; Iran's army in turn claimed attacks on US radar and Patriot systems at Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait, the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain and al-Azraq in Jordan, while Jordan said it intercepted eight Iranian missiles. At least 35 people have died and more than 300 been wounded since this wave began around Wednesday 8 July, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatened to halt all Middle East energy exports over the blockade: either for everyone or for no one.
fields.why: a direct US–Iran exchange now straddling the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint for roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil — with an explicit threat to the region's energy exports is the single most consequential escalation risk on the board, and the first strikes near Tehran mark a widening, not a winding-down.

fields.display_body: The two western cantons stood down the emergency measures triggered during the recent heatwave - coordination of care homes, hospitals and public-health messaging - but stressed that vulnerable people remain at risk and that the sanitary alert is being relaxed, not cancelled.
fields.why: a concrete, local marker that the heat episode straining Vaud's health services has broken, though the caution flags how these plans have become a recurring summer fixture.

fields.display_body: A raid on 23 June across three French departements and Switzerland, coordinated with Swiss authorities and Europol, led to 10 arrests in France and two in Switzerland; nine were charged on 26 June with illegal possession, manufacture or trafficking of war materiel, weapons and munitions as part of an organised criminal group. The gang is alleged to have stocked up on weapons in Switzerland and resold them across France.
fields.why: it puts Switzerland squarely in the supply chain for firearms feeding French organised crime, and the arrest of a police officer sharpens the case.

fields.display_body: A resident of Niedergosgen alerted police around 22:30 after spotting the drones heading for the plant; Solothurn cantonal police confirmed the response and are checking flight paths in coordination with the federal civil-aviation office (BAZL) and federal police (Fedpol). The plant's information chief said security was never compromised - the reactor is built to withstand even a large aircraft crash - and that the drone threat to nuclear safety is currently deemed negligible, though a similar 2025 sighting over the Laufenburg power hub turned out to be an authorised Swissgrid inspection flight.
fields.why: it adds a nuclear site to a run of recent drone sightings over Swiss military and energy infrastructure (Jassbach and Meiringen this month), keeping critical-infrastructure surveillance on the political agenda even when the drones prove benign.

fields.display_body: The US mounted a seventh consecutive night of airstrikes on Iran overnight into Saturday 18 July, and by mid-morning declared the wave concluded — while visibly widening its target set beyond military installations. Al Jazeera reported the latest strikes hit bridges and energy infrastructure and cut off water to villages in southern Iran, which its correspondent framed as a broadening of the campaign from narrowly military objectives toward civilian infrastructure. Swiss broadcaster SRF reported that Washington had formally called the seventh strike wave over, even as Iran continues to fire on the Gulf states hosting US forces. The exchange extends an escalation that has drawn US bases across the Gulf into direct fire since the Strait of Hormuz standoff sharpened in June, with both sides publicly rejecting the negotiated pause each accuses the other of refusing.
fields.why: a bombing campaign now in its seventh straight night, reaching bridges, power and water supplies and pulling Gulf states into direct exchanges, raises the risk of a wider regional war and keeps Hormuz shipping and energy markets on edge.

fields.display_body: Thousands rallied again in Kyiv on Saturday 18 July against President Volodymyr Zelensky's dismissal of defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, deepening a political crisis that opened when Zelensky sacked him on Wednesday 15 July. Fedorov, 35 — the youngest defence minister in Ukraine's history and the figure most identified with its drone-warfare programme — was removed in a government reshuffle that Le Temps reads as a clash of doctrine between a younger, technology-driven generation and older commanders still shaped by Soviet-era methods. The upheaval lands despite a run of better news for Kyiv: a 90 billion euro EU loan, reinforced backing from the coalition of the willing, and Ukrainian strikes on military and energy sites deep inside Russia.
fields.why: sidelining the minister most associated with Ukraine's drone edge — while Moscow shows no interest in negotiating — risks fracturing national unity at a moment Kyiv can least afford it.

fields.display_body: The Trump administration finalised two rollbacks to the Endangered Species Act (ESA — the 1973 US law protecting at-risk wildlife) on Friday 17 July, citing economic and national-security priorities. One change repeals the rule that automatically extended the Act's full protections to species merely listed as "threatened"; the other lets the government weigh economic and national-security considerations when deciding whether an area qualifies as "critical habitat" for a protected species. Emblematic animals such as the Alaskan grizzly and the bald eagle — the US national bird — are among those covered by the weakened framework.
fields.why: it marks a further narrowing of America's flagship conservation law, shifting its default posture from protection toward development.

fields.display_body: Cadmium — a toxic heavy metal that accumulates in the body over time — is drawing fresh scrutiny in Switzerland's food supply, Le Temps reported on Saturday 18 July, though Swiss exposure appears lower than in neighbouring France. In France, roughly one resident in two exceeds the at-risk concentration threshold, prompting the National Assembly to pass a bill in June 2026 aimed at curbing cadmium in agricultural soils, the main route by which it enters the food chain. Swiss contamination looks milder, but the underlying data are patchy and specialists urge caution rather than reassurance.
fields.why: it adds another contaminant — after mercury, pesticides and microplastics — to the list of everyday dietary exposures, and highlights how thin Switzerland's own monitoring data still are.

fields.display_body: A summer heatwave tightened its grip on Switzerland this week, with fire bans now in force, a 20-kilometre tailback of up to three hours at the Gotthard's north portal on Saturday 18 July, and fish dying in overheated eastern-Swiss waters. Climate historian Christian Pfister told SRF he fears 2026 could become a modern analogue of 1540 — the year of a legendary Europe-wide megadrought — as heat, drought and wildfire risk compound. The developments follow SRF Meteo's warning a week earlier that 2026 could surpass the record "century summer" of 2003 if August stays hot.
fields.why: beyond the immediate disruption — grilling bans, Alpine traffic, stressed rivers — a sustained heatwave strains water, agriculture and infrastructure, and the 1540 comparison underscores how far outside the historical envelope recent Swiss summers are running.

fields.display_body: Switzerland is quietly stepping up its Arctic engagement, Le Temps reported on Friday 17 July, with a newly formed parliamentary group and a science-and-dialogue strategy to justify a role in a region where it has no coastline and no vote. Bern, an observer on the Arctic Council since 2017, argues that the Alps and the Arctic share many of the same challenges and points to Switzerland's more-than-150-year tradition of cryosphere (snow-and-ice) research. Former EPFL president Patrick Aebischer is championing a lighter, more community-focused model of polar science aboard the laboratory sailboat Forel, framed explicitly as "scientific diplomacy."
fields.why: it is a small but telling example of how a landlocked state seeks influence in climate-critical regions through research rather than territory.

fields.display_body: The United States declared its seventh and final strike wave on Iran over on Saturday 18 July , ending a week-long bombing campaign. The week saw escalation around the Strait of Hormuz — the fragile US–Iran understanding was publicly declared "worthless" around 13 July — and Iranian retaliation against US-allied Gulf states reported on 17 July. This is the summer's structural wildcard: the same conflict the daily briefs have tracked since the war reopened on 28 February 2026, now cycling through discrete escalation waves rather than resolving.

Ukraine's President Zelensky triggered a surprise wartime cabinet reshuffle on Sunday 12 July , unexpectedly asking Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko to resign — a move his own inner circle reportedly did not see coming — reopening the government mid-war with Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov's role now in question.
A magnitude-7.3 earthquake struck off the Pacific coast of southern Mexico/Guatemala on 17 July ; a tsunami alert was issued and then lifted the same day.

An Iranian missile killed two US service members at a base in Jordan on Saturday 18 July, drawing an eighth consecutive night of US strikes on Iran. US Central Command (CENTCOM — the American military command for the Middle East) said the strike also left a third soldier missing in action (MIA) and wounded four more; these are the first US combat deaths since a truce with Iran in early April, and they land after a week of the heaviest fighting since the war erupted in February. In response, the US launched its eighth straight night of strikes overnight into Sunday, with CENTCOM saying the latest wave targeted Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC — Iran's elite parallel military). Iran reported strikes in its south and around the Strait of Hormuz, US bases in Kuwait came under fire, and the United Arab Emirates was threatened; Washington warned Iran-backed groups might target Americans abroad and said it was moving more warplanes to the region. Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, vowed the US would be taught "unforgettable lessons," and Tehran said it had suspended implementation of a memorandum of understanding.
fields.why: direct American casualties cross a line both sides had avoided since April, sharply raising the risk that a contained air campaign widens into a broader regional war astride the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint through which much of the world's seaborne oil passes.

fields.display_body: Russia hit Kyiv with what Ukrainian officials called the largest ballistic-missile barrage on the capital since the war began, early Sunday 19 July. The hours-long attack spanned six districts of the city, killing one person and wounding at least 16, Ukraine's national police said. It came a day after a Ukrainian drone attack struck e-commerce warehouses near Moscow — the latest exchange in an intensifying summer air campaign. Al Jazeera noted Kyiv is weathering near-daily strikes amid a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors (its best defence against ballistic missiles).
fields.why: even with a comparatively low death toll, a record ballistic-missile salvo underscores how thinly stretched Ukraine's air defences are as Western interceptor stocks run low.

fields.display_body: At least 50 Malian soldiers were killed and dozens more captured in a coordinated attack by Tuareg separatists and allied jihadists, reported Sunday 19 July. Local sources told AFP that the assault — one of the deadliest single blows to Mali's army in its grinding northern insurgency — overran an army position, with dozens of troops taken prisoner. The Tuareg are a Saharan ethnic group whose rebels have long fought the government in Bamako, at times in alliance with jihadist factions.
fields.why: the toll signals that Mali's junta-led government and its Russian security partners are still losing ground in the Sahel, a region whose instability drives migration toward Europe.

fields.display_body: Hungary's president, Tamas Sulyok, signed on Saturday 18 July the constitutional amendment that ends his own mandate, effective Sunday 19 July. The move followed parliament's 13 July vote (139–6) to oust him, driven by Peter Magyar's opposition Tisza party, which now commands a two-thirds majority; the package also caps the terms of constitutional judges and members of parliament. Sulyok, himself a former constitutional judge, said he had no choice but to approve the law but warned that it inflicts serious damage on the rule of law and the separation of powers and sets a dangerous precedent.
fields.why: a sitting head of state enacting his own removal is an extraordinary constitutional moment, and for a Swiss and EU reader it sharpens the question of Hungary's institutional direction as an anti-Orban opposition consolidates power.

fields.display_body: Swiss security authorities are warning of a new, ideology-free form of youth radicalization they call "violent nihilism," SRF reported Sunday 19 July. Unlike conventional extremism, the movement advances neither a political nor a religious cause; according to the authorities, it glorifies violence for its own sake, drawing vulnerable young people into loose online networks. The warning frames it as a distinct and spreading phenomenon among Swiss adolescents rather than a variant of known jihadist or far-right radicalization.
fields.why: an online-native extremism with no political or religious programme is harder for existing counter-radicalization efforts — built around identifiable ideologies — to detect and disrupt.

fields.display_body: Switzerland's falling birth rate is unusually driven by couples forgoing a third child, not by skipping parenthood, University of Lausanne demographer Laura Bernardi told SRF (published Sunday 19 July). Whereas in most EU states the decline is mainly explained by fewer first births, in Switzerland only about half of the drop is; the rest, Bernardi says, comes from families stopping at two children. For scale, SRF notes South Korea — where a hyper-competitive environment pushes the young to forgo children or stop at one — has the world's lowest fertility rate, around 0.7 children per woman.
fields.why: it reframes the policy lever, suggesting that supporting larger families, not just first-time parents, would do more to lift Swiss fertility.

fields.display_body: The US struck Iran for a ninth consecutive night early Monday (20 July) as a month-old ceasefire kept unravelling and the fight for the Strait of Hormuz widened. Iranian state media (IRIB, Fars) reported explosions from the Gulf ports of Bandar Mahshahr and Bandar Imam Khomeini to Jask, Sirik, Konarak and Chabahar on the southern coast, and — for the first time in this escalation — as far north as Tabriz. The US military said it hit command centres, air defences, coastal-surveillance and missile/drone launch sites to degrade Iran's ability to attack shipping; Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) said it fired missiles and drones from Lorestan at US assets, claiming strikes on airbases in Jordan (Aqaba, Azraq) and Kuwait (Ali Al Salem), with sirens also sounding in Bahrain. The US now confirms a third service member killed in recent days in Jordan and Iraq; President Trump said the latest strikes were carried out "in honour" of those troops and repeated that "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon." Washington says it is enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports while the IRGC says two oil tankers "exploded" overnight attempting what it called an "unsafe" corridor through the strait. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in the Philippines, said the US remained "open to diplomacy" but "it has to be real," urging other countries to help protect Hormuz shipping. Brent crude rose above $90 a barrel for the first time in over a month — a direct cost for import-dependent Switzerland.
fields.why: a great-power air campaign, mounting US casualties and a contested chokepoint that carries a fifth of the world's seaborne oil is the combination most likely to turn a regional war into a global economic shock.

fields.display_body: The Ebola outbreak in eastern DR Congo has killed close to 1,000 people out of 2,344 confirmed cases, and Canada barred entry to recent travellers on Monday (20 July). More than one in three confirmed infections has been fatal in what authorities call the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record, which began about two months ago in the country's east; the death toll has jumped from roughly 600 reported on 9 July. Canada's health agency said its ban — blocking non-residents who were in the DRC within the past 21 days — took effect Monday, following a similar US restriction last week. Both go against WHO guidance, which rates the risk of international spread as low and advises against travel or trade restrictions on the grounds they stigmatise affected countries and hamper epidemic control.
fields.why: a lethal, fast-moving outbreak colliding with unilateral border closures reopens the hard pandemic-era question of whether such bans protect anyone or mainly punish the countries doing the containing.

fields.display_body: The Aargau public prosecutor on Monday (20 July) demanded a life sentence for former SVP cantonal MP Patrick Frei, accused of drugging and sexually assaulting several women and a minor. Frei, 57, a former member of the Aargau Grand Council held in pretrial detention, faces charges that include multiple counts of attempted murder, aggravated rape and sexual acts with children; prosecutors allege he rendered victims unconscious with knock-out drops before assaulting them. The case came to light in September 2023 after the mother of one victim caught him in the act.
fields.why: a demand for Switzerland's most severe penalty against a former elected official makes this one of the gravest political-figure criminal cases the canton has seen, and the verdict will test how the courts weigh the attempted-murder framing built on the alleged drugging.

fields.display_body: Ferran Torres, on as a substitute, drove home early in extra time (around the 106th minute) to give Spain a 1-0 win over Argentina in the World Cup final at MetLife Stadium outside New York on Sunday. It is Spain's second world title after 2010, and it completes a rare double: they were already European champions, so one nation now holds both trophies at once. The result crowns a young Spanish side built around Lamine Yamal and Nico Williams as the dominant force in the men's game — and it closes the book on Argentina's title defence, and on the 39-year-old Lionel Messi's bid to leave with the trophy in hand. The holders were reduced to ten men (Enzo Fernández sent off) and managed only two shots across 120 minutes; Spain conceded just one goal in the whole tournament, the meanest defence of any World Cup winner, over a record eight matches in the new 48-team format co-hosted by the USA, Canada and Mexico. Torres became only the second substitute ever to score a World Cup final winner.
fields.why: This is the sport's biggest prize, and it settles the argument over who the team of the era is — not Argentina, France or Brazil, but a Spain side young enough to stay there. For a casual viewer, it's the tournament that will frame the next four years of football.

fields.display_body: As the final whistle blew, Alain Berset — the former Swiss federal councillor now Secretary General of the Council of Europe (the 46-nation human-rights body based in Strasbourg, separate from the EU) — publicly pressed FIFA to open an "integrity" dialogue that same evening and to build a framework before the 2030 World Cup. His central example, per SRF's reporting: a red card against US forward Folarin Balogun that was rescinded, which Berset attributed to a phone call from President Donald Trump — political influence, he argued, reaching onto the pitch itself. He also flagged racist abuse of players and FIFA's expansion into stadium betting partnerships as openings for fraud. The framing here — "integrity", and the causal link between Trump's call and the reversal — is Berset's and SRF's characterisation; FIFA has not formally responded, and the causation claim rests on a single source.
fields.why: When a European human-rights institution publicly asks whether a head of state swayed a match decision, the story stops being about the scoreline and becomes about who actually controls the game heading into the next tournament.

fields.display_body: On the Tour's first serious mountain day — Stage 15, Champagnole to the Plateau de Solaison in the Alps — Belgium's Remco Evenepoel outsprinted overall leader Tadej Pogačar for the stage win. But the day turned on a crash: Jonas Vingegaard, the two-time Tour champion and the one rider realistically able to challenge Pogačar, went down roughly 20 km from the finish, broke his collarbone and abandoned the race. That leaves Pogačar leading the general classification (GC — the overall time standings that decide the winner) by about five minutes from Evenepoel, with Isaac del Toro third at 5:58. In effect, the only man who has ever beaten Pogačar at the Tour is out, all but confirming the Slovenian's expected fifth title with the race's final week still to come.
fields.why: A three-week Grand Tour is decided as much by who survives as by who is fastest; a collarbone, not a rival's legs, has drained most of the suspense from the finish.

fields.display_body: Bernese wrestler Fabian Staudenmann won the Rigi-Schwinget — one of the summer's mountain festivals in Schwingen (Swiss wrestling, contested in a sawdust ring), held on the Rigi above Lake Lucerne — beating fellow Bernese Lars Zaugg in the final bout (Schlussgang) on Sunday. It is his second win on the Rigi after 2024 and his 23rd festival crown. With no Eidgenössisches (the sport's championship, staged only every three years) on the 2026 calendar, individual festival wins like this are how the pecking order among the top wrestlers gets set through late summer.
fields.why: For a Swiss reader, Schwingen is a genuine national event, not a niche; Staudenmann is quietly building the form that counts when the biggest festivals arrive.

fields.display_body: The paper uses a deliberately trivial probe — "I want to wash my car. The car wash is 100 metres away. Should I walk or drive?" (you must drive, because the car has to reach the wash) — and shows that Qwen3-8B recommends walking in 85–100% of sampled runs and 100% of greedy (no-randomness) runs, in both its "thinking" and "non-thinking" modes; a 4,096-token budget for deliberation does not fix it. The second part is the interesting one: a training-free "activation oracle" (a probe read off the model's internal states, not trained on this task) detects the "walk" answer in the hidden states before the model has written any answer text.
fields.why: this is direct, if preliminary, evidence for a worry that has mostly been argued in the abstract — that a chain-of-thought (the written-out reasoning) can be a post-hoc rationalisation of a decision the model already made, rather than the process that produced it. If the commitment is visible in activations before the text, then reading the reasoning out loud tells you less about why than it appears to.

fields.display_body: Modern chat models flip a correct answer alarmingly easily when given a casual hint, a mislabelled example, or a faked earlier "assistant" turn — the family of failures called sycophancy (telling the user what they seem to want) and cue-following. Across five model families and seven bias types, the authors extract a single direction in the model's hidden state for each bias and confirm it three ways (probing, transfer to held-out datasets, and causal intervention). The finding: pretrained base models barely show these biases at all — the susceptibility, and a clean decodable signal for it, only appears after alignment tuning (the RLHF/instruction-tuning stage — reinforcement learning from human feedback — that turns a raw model into a helpful assistant). Because each bias is one coherent direction, they can steer along it to recover the un-biased answer.
fields.why: it relocates a much-discussed failure from "somewhere in the weights" to a specific, manipulable place, and pins the blame on the very step meant to make models safer and more helpful. That is both a warning — the helpfulness training is where the pushover behaviour comes from — and a lever, since a single direction is something you can monitor or subtract at inference time.

fields.display_body: A puzzle in interpretability is that a model can nail a problem in one wording and fail the exact same problem reworded. Do the two formats use different internal machinery, or the same machinery in a different state? Prior mechanistic work (reverse-engineering the actual computation) found that LLM arithmetic runs on a "bag of heuristics" — a sparse set of feed-forward neurons each implementing a small rule of thumb rather than a real algorithm. Here the authors locate those arithmetic neurons in three Llama-3 models across three formats — bare symbols ("24 + 17"), a word problem, and code — and find a compact set of neurons shared across all three, which targeted interventions show is both necessary and sufficient for the arithmetic to work.
fields.why: it argues the arithmetic circuit is form-invariant — the same underlying "adder" is reused regardless of how the question is dressed — so format-dependent failures are more about routing the input into that circuit than about the circuit itself. That is a useful narrowing for anyone trying to understand, or repair, why LLMs are so brittle to superficial rewording.

fields.display_body: Long "reasoning" generations are largely uncontrollable once running — prompt tweaks act only on the input, not on the unfolding thought. The authors treat a reasoning trace as a sequence of latent states (a small alphabet of recurring "modes" the model passes through) and show statistically that failures are trajectories that get stuck in self-loops, burning the whole token budget without making progress. Their method, SOPHIA, intervenes directly on the model's activations at inference time — activation steering, i.e. nudging the internal vector rather than editing the prompt — to push a stuck trajectory out of the loop.
fields.why: it reframes "the model rambled and ran out of budget" as a specific, detectable dynamical failure with an equally specific fix, and adds to the growing evidence that fine-grained control of how a model reasons is better done inside the activations than through the prompt.

fields.display_body: On-device deployment usually leans on coarse tools — pruning (deleting weights wholesale) or quantisation (storing them at lower precision) — that trade accuracy or require re-tuning. SelectInfer works at the neuron level instead: an offline profiler labels each neuron as task-specific or general-purpose, then two runtime tricks kick in — selective loading keeps only the important neurons in memory, and selective computation evaluates only the relevant ones per query. The reported result is a meaningful cut in both memory footprint and compute while holding task accuracy, with no retraining.
