fields.why: it is a concrete lever for running capable models on phones and laptops, where memory — not just speed — is the binding constraint, and it does so without the accuracy hit or extra training that pruning and quantisation typically demand.

fields.display_body: Transformers compute in a fixed stack of layers, and shallow versus deep blocks tend to specialise into different roles. Möbius Learning challenges the assumption that a block's role must be tied to its position: different data streams are sent through cyclically shifted block orders, so the same group of blocks is applied early for some data and late for others, forcing it to be good in both a shallow and a deep role ("depth-role superposition"). In four-worker experiments with a 124-million-parameter GPT-2-scale model on 2.5 billion tokens, this counter-intuitively achieves lower validation loss than a fixed-order looped Transformer.
fields.why: beyond the surprising result that blocks need not keep a fixed depth role, the structure is a natural fit for memory-limited distributed training — each worker stores one block group rather than the whole stack, and the raw data stays local — which is exactly the regime that makes training large models on modest hardware hard. This is flagged as a preliminary technical report.

fields.display_body: "Progressive disclosure" is the pattern behind Agent Skills — packaging expertise in folders an agent opens on demand, revealing only what a query needs, from a one-line description down to specific passages. Practitioners adopted it for book-length tasks on anecdote alone; this is the first controlled study, comparing raw-document navigation and several Skills designs against a classical retriever across three agent harnesses and three model families. The result is nuanced: on a single book the gain depends entirely on the harness — large when the agent navigates raw text poorly, near zero when a strong agent already retrieves well; across many books, raw navigation collapses while one level of disclosure degrades gracefully and pulls ahead; a second, deeper routing level never helps and sometimes breaks accuracy.
fields.why: for anyone building agents (this reader's day job included), it is a rare controlled answer to a design choice usually made on vibes — "progressive disclosure buys context, not intelligence," redundant while a strong agent can find the passage itself and decisive only once the corpus outgrows what it can read. And one level is enough.

fields.display_body: Most AI-safety evaluations stop at text: does the model say something dangerous? This work — a specialised attacker model, Intern-BioBreaker, plus an end-to-end framework — pushes past that. It generates targeted jailbreak prompts to elicit operational biological guidance or harmful sequence-level outputs, then carries selected outputs forward into actual DNA synthesis, expression in a host organism, and protein verification. The reported findings are sobering: near-saturated attack-success rates against both open-weight and proprietary frontier models, a case where GPT-5.5 could be induced to produce modified viral candidate sequences whose translated proteins showed stronger receptor binding, and confirmation that some model-generated designs can be physically realised, not just written down.
fields.why: it closes the gap between a jailbreak on paper and a demonstrated physical hazard, which is the distinction that matters for biosecurity policy. The authors' own conclusion is a call for stronger biological red-teaming and, crucially, nucleic-acid-synthesis screening — the choke point that sits between a dangerous sequence and a real one. Treat the specifics as the authors' own reported evaluation.

fields.display_body: Per The Information (as reported by The Decoder), Google is developing an internal server chip, "Frozen v2," that hard-wires parts of the Gemini model's architecture — the structural blueprint, not the trained weights — directly into the hardware, reportedly making it 6–10× more efficient at serving responses than current TPUs, with deployment targeted from 2028. An earlier design attributed to Jeff Dean would have frozen the weights themselves but was scrapped as too inflexible; embedding the architecture instead lets new weights still be loaded. Because it only works while Google keeps that architecture, it is meant for internal use, not sale.
fields.why: inference cost increasingly sets AI margins, so a chip that runs Gemini far cheaper is a competitive lever against OpenAI and Anthropic, not just an engineering curiosity. It also marks a shift from general-purpose accelerators toward model-specific silicon — powerful when a model architecture is stable, brittle when it isn't. This rests on a single paywalled report; the numbers and 2028 timeline are unverified. _Reported 2026-07-20._ ---

fields.display_body: At current exchange rates the gain narrowed to 2%, dragged by a negative currency effect of nearly 200 million francs; the Biel-based group led by Nick Hayek pointed to a strong spring acceleration while acknowledging that profitability remains under pressure.
fields.why: Swatch is a bellwether for the Swiss watch industry, and a rebound after a weak stretch signals firmer demand — though the currency drag underscores how the strong franc keeps eating into exporters' results.

fields.display_body: The US–Israel war on Iran widened into the Red Sea on Tuesday 21 July as Yemen's Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, closing the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Two oil tankers carrying Saudi crude toward Asia turned back after the announcement, compounding disruption already hitting the Strait of Hormuz — the two chokepoints together carry a large share of seaborne oil. The US said it had concluded its 11th round of strikes on Iran and Tehran retaliated; Washington is reportedly weighing an attack on Iran's "Pickaxe Mountain," believed to be an underground uranium-enrichment site. Testifying to senators on Wednesday 22 July, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth put the war's cost to the US at $37.5bn so far and requested $87.6bn more, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US remains "open" to negotiations but that Iran is "not serious."
fields.why: a second closed chokepoint turns a regional war into a direct shock to global energy shipping, and the funding request signals Washington is bracing for a long campaign, not a quick strike.

fields.display_body: President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed the commander-in-chief of Ukraine's armed forces, Oleksandr Syrsky, on Tuesday 21 July, and named the popular joint-forces commander Mykhailo Drapaty to replace him. The move follows the 15 July sacking of young defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov — the architect of Ukraine's drone force — which set off mass protests in Kyiv; demonstrators had accused the military leadership of wasting lives. Le Temps frames the shake-up as Zelensky sidelining modernisers in favour of "the old guard."
fields.why: replacing both the defence minister and the top general inside a week, under public pressure, points to a real doctrinal fight over how Ukraine fights the war — and rare open dissent at home.

fields.display_body: The Trump administration is expected to announce Wednesday 22 July a deal under which US firms would build a uranium-enrichment complex in Saudi Arabia, giving the kingdom a civil nuclear programme. Officials stress the programme is meant for civilian use; critics warn that endorsing enrichment on Saudi soil — as the US is actively bombing Iran to stop its own enrichment — could accelerate a regional arms race.
fields.why: enrichment is the dual-use step that separates a power reactor from a bomb, so a US-blessed Saudi enrichment plant reshapes the Gulf's proliferation math at the worst possible moment.

fields.display_body: The French Parliament definitively adopted on Tuesday 21 July a law barring under-15s from social media — a European first — with the ban set to take effect in September. The Macron-backed text requires platforms to verify users' ages but sets no penalty for families, a gap that drew criticism as unworkable. This finalises the bill the two chambers were only scheduled to vote on a day earlier.
fields.why: it is the first hard national age floor for social media in the EU, and a live test of whether platform-side age verification can be enforced at all — with implications for how neighbouring states, including Switzerland, regulate minors online.

fields.display_body: Donald Trump's threatened 100% tariff on imported generic drugs, announced Tuesday 21 July and slated to start in 2028, lands squarely on Swiss-based Sandoz. The world's leading generics maker manufactures largely in Europe, so a US import levy — which Washington says is meant to relocate production stateside and which could rise to 200% in 2029 — would hit its US business hard.
fields.why: generics are a thin-margin, high-volume business, and a tariff of this size is less a price signal than a demand to rebuild supply chains, a direct threat to a major Swiss pharma employer.

fields.display_body: Geneva's justice system has suspended the canton's contested law banning long swimwear — including the burkini — in public pools, granting suspensive effect to an appeal. The law took force at the end of May but is now blocked pending the case; it is also being challenged by five communes, among them the city of Geneva itself.
fields.why: the suspension is the first serious legal setback for one of Switzerland's most divisive recent cantonal measures, and pits the canton against its own largest city.

fields.display_body: Swiss air-navigation provider Skyguide faces a structural deficit of about CHF 40 million a year from 2030, and transport politicians are pushing for new revenue sources. Skyguide lives mainly on fees airlines pay for landings and overflights, with the Confederation — its main shareholder — already contributing over CHF 120 million for special tasks such as military air control and services in cross-border airspace; that no longer covers costs. Ideas floated include recovering fees from foreign users of Swiss-controlled airspace or charging passengers directly, alongside a federal cost-cutting programme.
fields.why: the funding gap forces a choice between higher travel costs and cuts at an operator that has had high-profile outages, touching both flight safety and ticket prices.

fields.display_body: In the quantum Hall effect - the regime where a cold two-dimensional electron sheet in a strong magnetic field carries current losslessly along its edges - electrical conduction comes in exact, universal quantized steps. Whether heat is carried the same universal way in the richer Hofstadter states (the fractal energy spectrum electrons form when a magnetic field and a periodic moire lattice act on them together) had never been tested. Using Johnson-noise thermometry - reading temperature off the faint electrical noise that any warm conductor emits - the team measured the thermal conductance of quantum-Hall, Chern-insulator, and interaction-driven symmetry-broken states in a bilayer-graphene/boron-nitride superlattice (moire wavelength about 14 nm), and found it quantized in units of the thermal conductance quantum, tracking each state's Chern number (the integer that labels its topology).
fields.why: it shows these exotic topological states move heat as cleanly and universally as they move charge, confirming their fundamental nature and giving a probe of edge modes that ordinary electrical measurements can miss.

fields.display_body: Science reports new high-pressure laboratory measurements putting the melting point of iron at inner-core-boundary conditions at roughly 4,420–5,220 K — more than 1,000 °C below the ~5,500 °C usually quoted — implying a cooler core than the standard picture. The team squeezed iron between diamond anvils to near two million atmospheres (comparable to the outer core) and, instead of laser-heating it, drove it with microsecond electrical pulses for tighter temperature control. A cooler core is more permissive of a thermally driven geodynamo (the churning liquid-iron engine that generates Earth's magnetic field): per the report, core cooling alone could have powered the field for most of Earth's history, until the solid inner core began to freeze a little over half a billion years ago. I could not reach the primary paper or the article's full text from the sandbox, so this rests on Science's account via search snippet — treat the exact figures as provisional pending the paper.
fields.why: the core's temperature sets the energy budget for Earth's magnetic shield and the age of the solid inner core; shaving 1,000 °C off it reshuffles both.

fields.display_body: Naked mole-rats are one of the very few eusocial mammals: a single queen breeds while every other female stays infertile, and how the queen enforces that had been unclear. This study names the signal — isopropyl myristate, a low-volatility ester (a waxy, barely-evaporating oily molecule) strongly enriched in queens and nearly absent from non-breeders. Olfactory neurons in the nose and brain detect it; exposure shifts the hormones prolactin and progesterone in subordinates to suppress their reproduction and provokes avoidance in high-ranking rivals. In behavioural tests, adding the ester daily to a queenless colony prevented a new queen from emerging, while withdrawing it triggered aggression and reproductive competition. The same molecule showed up in breeding females of related Fukomys mole-rats, hinting the mechanism is shared across the group.
fields.why: it gives a concrete molecular handle — a chemical the animals can smell — on how a mammalian society centrally controls who gets to reproduce, rather than chalking it up to social stress alone.

fields.display_body: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) has been understudied genetically and often framed as purely a product of environment. This genome-wide association study — a scan of the whole genome for common DNA variants statistically linked to a trait — pooled 12,339 cases against about 1.04 million controls, with a separate replication sample, and identified 11 independent genomic loci and 9 risk genes. It reports a SNP-based heritability of 17.3% (the share of variation these common variants can account for) and polygenic scores that predict about 4.6% of the risk — a real biological signal but far from an individual-level test. All participants were of European ancestry, a genuine limitation on how broadly the results generalise, and the signals overlap with those of other psychiatric and some physical conditions.
fields.why: it is the first robust evidence of a common-variant genetic contribution to a heavily stigmatised condition, supporting a biological component and shared architecture with other disorders — without implying any near-term diagnostic use.

fields.display_body: Astronomers have directly imaged a third planet around Beta Pictoris, a young star 63 light-years away whose disk and planets are a benchmark for how planetary systems form. Direct imaging — photographing a planet's own light right next to its far brighter host — normally only works for bright, massive planets, so Beta Pictoris d is a milestone: it is about 100 times fainter than the famous Beta Pic b and, corrected for distance, the faintest exoplanet yet imaged from Earth. It is a gas giant of roughly 2.4 Jupiter masses (against ~10 for b and c) on a much wider orbit. The team spotted it with the Very Large Telescope's ERIS instrument, then found it lurking in archival VLT/SPHERE images going back 11 years; an independent group led by Aidan Gibbs (University of California) detected the same planet with JWST.
fields.why: Beta Pictoris becomes only the second system, after HR 8799, with more than two directly imaged planets — a natural laboratory for comparing worlds born from the same disk, and a taste of what ESO's Extremely Large Telescope should routinely reach.

fields.display_body: Reading an exoplanet atmosphere's metallicity (how enriched it is in elements heavier than hydrogen and helium) and its carbon-to-oxygen ratio — both clues to where in its disk the planet formed — usually demands several JWST instrument modes stitched across ~1–5 microns. This work shows both can be pulled from a single archival transit of the well-studied hot Jupiter WASP-39 b, taken with one NIRSpec mode, by importing a technique from ground-based astronomy: phase-resolved cross-correlation at the detector's native pixel resolution, which matches the full-resolution spectrum against molecular templates instead of collapsing it into a coarse light curve.
fields.why: if one instrument mode can do the job, JWST can characterise more planet atmospheres per hour of scarce telescope time — a practical multiplier for the field.

fields.display_body: India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised "fast-track courts" on Thursday (23 July) in his first public response to the youth-led "Cockroach" protests convulsing Delhi. The movement — organised as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) — erupted over leaked national medical-school entrance-exam papers and has occupied Parliament Street in central Delhi for three days, demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan; police have been accused of using pellet guns against demonstrators. "Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared," Modi wrote on X, pledging swift punishment for those behind the paper leaks.
fields.why: an exam-fraud grievance has escalated into the most sustained street challenge to Modi's government in years, testing how it handles a leaderless, student-driven movement.

fields.display_body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met for about half an hour in Manila on Thursday (23 July) on the sidelines of an ASEAN summit. Russia's foreign ministry said Lavrov "reaffirmed readiness" for a diplomatic settlement of the Ukraine war on the terms Presidents Trump and Putin discussed at their August 2025 Alaska meeting, while pressing that arming Kyiv was "unacceptable"; Rubio said afterwards the US remains ready to play a "constructive role" but declined to characterise Moscow's position. The meeting came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had spoken with US envoys to try to revive stalled talks.

Roche's first-half 2026 revenue slipped 2% in francs to CHF 30.4bn as the strong franc masked underlying growth, the Basel drugmaker reported Thursday (23 July). Stripped of currency effects, sales rose 6%; the pharmaceuticals division brought in CHF 23.6bn (down 1% year on year) while diagnostics fell 3% to CHF 6.7bn, dragged by a pricing reform in China. Core operating profit dipped 1% to CHF 11.9bn (up 10% at constant exchange rates) and core earnings per share fell 2% to CHF 10.85. Roche kept its full-year targets — mid-single-digit sales growth and high-single-digit core-EPS growth, both at constant rates.
fields.why: the split between the reported (–2%) and currency-adjusted (+6%) numbers is the recurring story of Swiss exporters this year — real growth abroad that a strong franc keeps shaving off the home-currency bottom line.

fields.display_body: Vaud-based Nestlé is spinning its bottled-water and premium-drinks arm — San Pellegrino, Perrier and Vaud's own Henniez — into a 50/50 joint venture with US private-equity firm Platinum Equity, the group announced Thursday (23 July). The new company, Peranel, values the division at €4.9bn (CHF 4.5bn) and hands day-to-day control to a specialist operator; the water business had been bruised by a scandal over the illegal use of filtration on mineral water sold as "natural". Nestlé frames the move as a milestone in a broader refocusing on its core food and beverage brands.
fields.why: it is one of the clearest steps yet in Nestlé's restructuring, and it partly hives off a Swiss household name (Henniez) into shared ownership with a US fund.

fields.display_body: MeteoSuisse warned Thursday (23 July) that Switzerland's drought could turn "locally very critical" without substantial rain, with parts of the country running a 60–90% rainfall deficit. The western Plateau, the Jura and the northern slopes of the eastern Alps are worst hit, according to the national drought platform (Plateforme nationale sur la sécheresse); rivers are dropping, Alpine pastures — including at Rossinière in Vaud's Pays-d'Enhaut — are stressed, and the shortfall feeds the same heat-and-drought that is driving the wildfires across southern Europe.

The US slapped a new 12.5% tariff on Swiss goods from 06:01 Swiss time on Friday 24 July, the top rate in a forced-labour trade action hitting 60 economies. The US Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, took "final action" under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act — the same durable legal tool Trump used against China in his first term — imposing 10% on partners that pledged to enforce a ban on imports made with forced labour and 12.5% on those USTR judged to have "failed to adopt" such a ban; Switzerland drew the higher rate. The levies took effect at 12:01am Washington time (04:01 GMT), the moment the temporary 10% worldwide tariff — a 150-day Section 122 stopgap adopted after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's broader IEEPA tariffs in February — expired. Swiss business reaction was immediate and hostile, with employers' groups quoted calling the move "unjustified and incomprehensible," and SRF noting Switzerland comes off worse than the EU, whose separate July trade deal caps most goods at a 15% all-inclusive ceiling.
fields.why: it lands a fresh, above-EU cost on Swiss exporters — pharma, machinery, watches — just as the prior tariff truce lapses, and reframes a US trade dispute as a human-rights enforcement claim against Swiss supply chains that Bern rejects.

fields.display_body: The Federal Office of Transport (BAV) told Switzerland's public-transport operators on Friday 24 July that they must guarantee analogue, cash-payable ticket options as machines and cash acceptance disappear. In a written directive to the industry, the BAV said every transport company must ensure that people who cannot or do not want to buy tickets digitally still have a way to obtain a valid one; spokesperson Andreas Windlinger said such passengers "should not be left behind." The rules are binding. The industry body Alliance SwissPass defended its digitalisation drive but said it would comply, pointing to existing options such as loading a ticket onto a SwissPass by phone in some regions.
fields.why: it is a concrete federal check on the cashless push in daily Swiss life, protecting older passengers and those without smartphones from being locked out of the transport network.

fields.display_body: US forces bombed Iran for a 13th consecutive night into Friday 24 July, Tehran rejected a ceasefire relayed by Iraq's prime minister, and Brent crude closed above $100 a barrel for the first time since May. US Central Command said it concluded its latest round of strikes at 01:00 GMT Friday, hitting military command centres, drone-storage sites, communications networks and coastal surveillance; Iranian media reported explosions across Khondab, Khorramabad, Bandar Abbas and Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran's Tasnim agency reporting four killed and five wounded near Ahvaz. Trump told Axios he might launch his largest strikes yet after Iran's retaliatory salvoes on Gulf US allies, which included hitting a telecoms tower in Kuwait, and Tehran warned it would hold accountable any country that supports a US strike. Shipping data showed just one tanker crossing Hormuz on Thursday — the lowest since 7 May — while Yemen's Houthis pressed a Red Sea blockade, though two Chinese supertankers carrying Saudi crude cleared the Bab al-Mandeb strait on Friday.
fields.why: an open-ended US bombing campaign, a collapsed ceasefire track and oil back over $100 point to a widening Gulf war whose energy-price shock reaches well beyond the region.

fields.display_body: Six candidates to succeed António Guterres as UN secretary-general set out their platforms on Thursday 23 July, with the world body facing a financial and confidence crisis. The contenders presented competing visions for reform ahead of a selection process that will decide the UN's leadership from January 2027; France 24 framed trust and credibility as the debate's dominant themes.
fields.why: the next secretary-general inherits a cash-strapped, authority-challenged UN at a moment of active great-power conflict, making the choice more consequential than the usual succession.

fields.display_body: A Saudi-led coalition struck the Houthi-held Yemeni port of Hodeida on Friday 24 July, and the Iran-backed Houthis vowed to retaliate on Saturday 25 July, pulling Saudi Arabia directly into the widening Gulf war. The strikes followed several days of Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea; Riyadh said it hit military targets and would "do everything necessary" to protect its shipping against a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade, while the Houthis said the strikes hit civilian infrastructure in Hodeida and injured two people. The flare-up opens a new front alongside the ongoing US–Iran confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz, and the UN warned on 24 July against a wider escalation as fighting intensified around the Red Sea — a corridor that normally carries a large share of world seaborne trade.
fields.why: a direct Saudi–Houthi exchange layered on top of the US–Iran war threatens both of the region's two critical maritime chokepoints (Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb) at once, and any sustained closure of Red Sea shipping feeds straight into global energy and freight costs.

fields.display_body: Wildfires across western France, central Spain and Italy have now forced roughly 200,000 people from their homes, authorities said Saturday 25 July, as separate blazes merged and hot, dry, windy conditions kept them out of control. In France's Gironde and Landes departments the fire drove mass evacuations around Bordeaux, while Spain — which declared its first-ever national wildfire emergency on Thursday 23 July over blazes near Madrid and in Ávila — and Italy continued to battle major fires amid a Europe-wide heatwave. DW reported conditions that made it "nearly impossible for firefighters to gain the upper hand."
fields.why: the evacuation total has roughly quadrupled in two days, marking one of the worst fire seasons on record for southern Europe and straining cross-border firefighting resources at peak summer.

fields.display_body: India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, announced his resignation on Saturday 25 July amid a youth-led protest movement that has occupied the Jantar Mantar grounds in New Delhi for 36 days. Pradhan's departure is the first cabinet-level concession to the "Cockroach" movement (the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party), with a second round of talks between the movement and the government scheduled and police tightening security as crowds are expected to swell over the weekend.
fields.why: a sitting minister stepping down over sustained street protest is a rare retreat for Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government and a test of whether the youth movement can convert pressure into policy change.

fields.display_body: The UN General Assembly voted 144 to 10 on Friday 24 July to reappoint Volker Türk as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights for a second four-year term, keeping the Geneva-based office in the hands of a diplomat who has repeatedly and sharply criticised both Russia's war in Ukraine and Israel's conduct in Gaza. The vote followed a debate with pointed criticism of the Austrian: Israel's representative accused Türk of lacking "professionalism and leadership" and of bias.
fields.why: the OHCHR is one of International Geneva's flagship institutions, and a strong endorsement re-anchors an outspoken human-rights mandate in the city even as the office draws fire from governments it scrutinises.

fields.display_body: Russia's embassy in Bern published a caustic communiqué claiming Switzerland's own human-rights record shows "serious deficiencies" and that its standing as a model country is "compromised," Le Temps reported. The statement — Moscow effectively lecturing Bern on rights — landed roughly two months before Switzerland's popular vote on the neutrality initiative, a context Le Temps flagged as pointed given the sharp Russia–Switzerland friction since the war in Ukraine.
fields.why: it is a piece of diplomatic pressure aimed at Swiss domestic debate, using human-rights framing to needle a country Moscow accuses of abandoning neutrality.

fields.display_body: A growing number of Swiss cantons have banned private fireworks for the 1 August national holiday, SRF reported Saturday 25 July, so that this year's Bundesfeier will be unusually quiet. With an absolute open-air fire ban or a forest-and-forest-edge fire ban already in force across most of the country for weeks amid an entrenched drought and heatwave, cantons are extending the restrictions to holiday fireworks to avoid sparking wildfires; some municipalities have gone further.
fields.why: it is a concrete, daily-life consequence of the drought reaching into a national tradition, and a signal of how deep the wildfire risk now runs across Switzerland.

fields.display_body: Andy Burnham took office as UK prime minister on Monday 20 July , succeeding Keir Starmer in a mid-term Labour handover and becoming Britain's seventh leader in a decade.

EU ambassadors agreed a 21st sanctions package against Russia on the morning of Thursday 23 July , after granting Greece a carve-out to keep exporting Russian LNG to non-EU buyers and freezing a scheduled rise in the oil price cap for a year.

Multimodal LLMs routinely give answers that contradict a scene's actual 3D layout — "spatial-reasoning hallucination" — and the authors show existing mitigations fail here because they never bridge flat 2D features to real 3D structure. Geo3R is a training-free, plug-and-play module that injects explicit geometric evidence and structured 3D reasoning to correct the three recurring triggers (perspective, object orientation, viewpoint change). Across three benchmarks spanning 18 tasks it substantially cuts spatial errors across several base models with no retraining.
fields.why: reliable "what's-in-front-of-what" reasoning is a prerequisite for vision models in robotics and AR, and a drop-in fix beats retraining.

fields.display_body: Advanced persistent threats (long, quiet cyber-intrusions) are hard to detect because only a sliver of log events are malicious and prior ML detectors depend on heavily curated data. CAPTAIN instead scores raw, minimally processed log lines by perplexity — how surprising each entry is to a general pretrained language model — while injecting compact "context tokens" so that surprise reflects recent history rather than each line in isolation. It matches strong baselines on APT benchmarks while needing far less hand-engineered preprocessing.
fields.why: it turns an off-the-shelf language model into a low-maintenance anomaly detector, cutting the pipeline-building cost that makes security ML expensive to run.

fields.display_body: The Shannon capacity of a graph is the best rate at which you can send information with zero errors over a noisy channel described by that graph — a hard limit computed over ever-larger "strong powers" of the graph. Even the humble 7-cycle C7 has an unknown exact capacity (the 5-cycle was famously nailed by Lovasz in 1979), so progress comes only from explicitly constructing large error-free codebooks. The authors build record independent sets — for example, one of size 134,753 inside the 10th power of C7 — raising the best-known lower bounds for C7, C11 and C13. The constructions were discovered through iterative prompting of a large language model, then verified by hand.
fields.why: it nudges a stubborn 45-year-old problem forward and is a clean demonstration of AI producing verifiable new mathematical objects — the benign face of this week's "checkable-artifact" thread.

fields.display_body: Unclonable encryption hides a message in a quantum state so that a thief who intercepts the ciphertext cannot split it into two copies that both later decrypt — a guarantee with no classical analog, rooted in quantum no-cloning. Every prior construction leaned on unproven computational hardness (e.g. "factoring is hard"). This paper gives an unconditional scheme for one-time encryption of a single-bit message: security is information-theoretic, holding even against an adversary with unlimited computing power, with efficient encryption/decryption and an exponentially small chance of a successful cloning attack.
fields.why: it shows a core quantum-cryptographic promise can rest purely on the laws of physics rather than on assumptions that a future algorithm might overturn — a foundational feasibility result.

fields.display_body: Brown dwarfs and gas giants can beam coherent radio waves whose cutoff frequency directly encodes the object's magnetic-field strength. Earlier cold "methane" dwarfs showed no cutoff up to 10 GHz, implausibly implying very strong fields. Observing a binary first found in an untargeted low-frequency survey (so its emission more likely traces the large-scale field), the authors detect a clean cutoff giving a polar surface field of about 126 gauss — below simple energy-balance dynamo predictions but matching a Lorentz–Coriolis scaling law, favouring one theory of how such objects generate magnetism.
fields.why: direct magnetic-field measurements for cold sub-stellar objects are rare, and this one discriminates between dynamo theories that also govern gas-giant planets.

fields.display_body: Two back-to-back Nature papers repurpose Cas12a2, an unusual CRISPR nuclease (an RNA-guided DNA-cutting protein) that, once it recognizes a target RNA, indiscriminately chops up all nearby DNA — so-called collateral cleavage. The teams programmed it to switch on only when it senses a cancer-specific transcript, then let it shred that cell's own chromatin, triggering a lethal DNA-damage response. This offers a route to hit "undruggable" mutations that have no drug-binding pocket — including mutant TP53 (altered in roughly 40–50% of cancers), KRAS point mutants, and HPV-infected cells — with no off-target activation reported. The work is in cultured yeast and human cells, so it is early-stage and far from patients.
fields.why: a fundamentally different way to kill cancer cells, keyed to what a cell's RNA says it is rather than to a surface it presents — potentially reaching mutations conventional drugs cannot touch.

fields.display_body: A van drove into a crowd at Berlin's Christopher Street Day (the city's Pride march) late on Saturday 25 July, killing one person and injuring 16, three of them life-threateningly. The vehicle, a white transporter, struck marchers around 22:00 near Potsdamer Platz in the Tiergarten, and the parade was called off. Berlin police say they identified a fleeing suspect overnight — a 21-year-old man reported by German outlets as Abdul B. — and a citywide manhunt is under way; police describe him as having links to what they call the "Islamist scene," a characterisation that comes from investigators and has not been confirmed by any court or established motive. Of the injured, eight are seriously and five lightly hurt.
fields.why: it is the latest in a run of deadly vehicle-ramming attacks in Germany, and both the target — a Pride event — and the still-unproven motive will shape a charged domestic debate over security and extremism; treat the early "Islamist" framing as a police working theory, not a settled fact.

fields.display_body: The UN warned on Friday 24 July against a wider escalation in the US–Iran war and flagged the risk to global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, as US strikes on Iran paused for a second day. The Strait is the narrow waterway carrying roughly a fifth of the world's oil; the warning came amid renewed Houthi attacks in the Red Sea. US Central Command, meanwhile, says its naval blockade of Iran "remains in force" — so the two-day lull in strikes is a pause, not a settlement, and earlier US framing of a "final" round of strikes has not held up.
fields.why: any closure of Hormuz or spread of the fighting to Red Sea shipping lanes would ripple straight into energy prices and supply chains far from the war zone.

fields.display_body: Brazil refused entry visas to two planned US envoys, accusing Washington of trying to influence its coming presidential election. The move deepens a rift between Brasília and Washington that already includes US tariffs on Brazilian goods, and it lands as Flávio Bolsonaro — a senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro — secured his party's nod to run against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
fields.why: it is an unusually direct rebuff of the US by a major non-aligned democracy, and signals how sharply the Trump administration's tariff-and-pressure approach is straining relations across the Americas.

fields.display_body: Breitling chief executive Georges Kern publicly appealed to Washington on Saturday 25 July to exempt Swiss watches from US tariffs, arguing that America has no watch industry to protect. In an interview with the NZZ am Sonntag, Kern said tariffs are "protectionism, but there are sectors the Americans have no need to protect because they simply don't have them," and that Swiss watches belong in that category. His plea follows the new 12.5% US duty on Swiss goods that took effect on Friday 24 July — imposed under a US "forced labour" rationale that Switzerland's business federation economiesuisse rejects as baseless, noting forced labour is already banned under Swiss constitutional and criminal law.
fields.why: it is the first prominent Swiss-industry attempt to carve out a sector-specific escape from the tariff, and shows exporters betting on lobbying rather than waiting on Bern's trade talks.

fields.display_body: Several Swiss cantons have issued explicit fireworks bans for the 1 August national holiday as a weeks-long drought keeps most of the country under open-fire restrictions. With near-total bans on open fires already in place across much of Switzerland — Zürich and Winterthur, for instance, prohibit even charcoal grilling in public — cantons have in recent days tightened the rules specifically for fireworks ahead of Saturday 1 August, meaning the traditional displays will be barred almost everywhere.
fields.why: it is a concrete, everyday sign of the same European heat-and-drought spell driving the wildfires abroad, and it reshapes how the country's biggest civic holiday will be marked this year.

fields.display_body: Wildfires around Bordeaux drove one of the largest evacuations in French history, with around 300,000 people now moved to safety across France and Spain and the flames roughly 15 km from the city. In southwest France the fire in the Gironde has burned more than 19,000 hectares and destroyed about 100 buildings since Wednesday, forcing some 220,000 people from their homes — 55,000 more ordered out around Bordeaux over the weekend, and 31,000 in neighbouring Landes; boats were used to evacuate holidaymakers from the Cap Ferret peninsula. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the blaze turned "extremely violent and unpredictable" overnight, the A63 motorway to Spain is shut over about 60 km, and nearly 100,000 hectares have burned nationwide since January — a historic record. In Spain the government declared a state of emergency around Madrid and in Ávila (where about 47,000 hectares burned), with roughly 90,000 people evacuated according to the interior ministry; El País reports the Madrid, Ávila and Toledo fires have covered some 77,000 hectares in all. A new heatwave with temperatures up to 40°C is forecast from Tuesday 28 July, threatening to worsen the fight.
fields.why: this is the sharp escalation of a fire emergency running across France, Spain and Italy since 23 July — the direct threat to Bordeaux, a metropolis of about 850,000, and the incoming heat push it well beyond the earlier evacuations.

fields.display_body: Iran warned Ukraine it will retaliate for a deadly strike on an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea , opening a new front that links the Russia–Ukraine war to the recent US–Israel conflict with Iran. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday 26 July that the Ukrainian attack the day before — which Iran says caused the ship to explode, killing one sailor and injuring several — "cannot go unanswered" and violated the UN Charter, and he accused Israel of provoking it to "drag Europe into its war." Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his forces had hit "vessels used in military cargo shipments involving Iran, as well as a warship" in long-range strikes, and accused Russia of feeding Iran satellite imagery of US facilities in the Gulf. Iran has summoned Ukraine's chargé d'affaires in Tehran, and a senior lawmaker said early Monday that Kyiv "may soon come to understand that Iran does not let actions go unanswered." Separately, the United States and Iran held off on fresh strikes for a second straight day, and oil prices eased.
fields.why: Kyiv striking an Iranian ship — over Tehran's supply of Shahed drones to Moscow since 2022 — risks pulling Iran directly into the Ukraine war just as a fragile pause in the US–Iran fighting takes hold.

fields.display_body: German police shot dead the suspect in Saturday night's Berlin Pride van-ramming attack , which Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said authorities are treating as an "Islamist terrorist attack." The suspect was killed in a police operation on Sunday 26 July after, police said, attacking officers with a bladed weapon; Dobrindt said there was no indication of a further threat. One person was killed and 29 injured — a higher toll than the 16 reported the day before — when the attacker drove a van into a crowd in Tiergarten Park, near the Christopher Street Day parade, one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ celebrations. Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged marchers "not to be intimidated," and the Brandenburg Gate was lit in the colours of the Pride flag for a candlelit vigil.
fields.why: the "Islamist terrorist" classification is the interior minister's characterisation and the investigation is early, but a deadly attack on a Pride event has already prompted German calls for tighter security.

fields.display_body: Thirty-four firefighters from French-speaking Switzerland — mostly Geneva, with crews from Vaud and Neuchâtel — arrived in the Gironde late on Saturday 25 July and worked through the night west of Cestas, about 10 km from Bordeaux's ring road, saving much of a solar-panel farm before the wind turned; further rotations are planned through 1 August. Separately, after France requested aircraft, the Swiss defence department (DDPS) decided to deploy two Super Puma helicopters to the Var department, expected to leave on Tuesday 28 July alongside a small humanitarian-aid rapid-response team.
fields.why: it is a concrete cross-border civil-protection commitment, and — with Switzerland's own forests parched — a marker of how the same drought conditions now stretch Alpine-region emergency services.

fields.display_body: Slovenia's Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) sealed his fifth Tour de France on the Champs-Élysées, drawing level with the sport's four all-time greats — Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain — as the only riders to win cycling's biggest race five times. It is his third in a row. As flagged here last week, the contest had effectively closed once his one real threat, two-time winner Jonas Vingegaard, abandoned with a broken collarbone on stage 15; his other rival, Belgium's Remco Evenepoel, finished second overall, 6 minutes 26 seconds back. Pogačar, 27, took five stage wins including a record ascent of Alpe d'Huez.
fields.why: Five wins puts Pogačar in the conversation as the greatest cyclist ever — but the reception is telling. He was booed by some fans during the race, less out of dislike than frustration that his dominance has drained the Tour of suspense. That tension — a generational champion whose brilliance makes the event less competitive — is now the sport's central question.

fields.display_body: Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix for his and McLaren's first victory of the 2026 season — a striking line to write about a team that dominated the sport a year ago. His race-long McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri led the first half after passing Norris at the start, but lost time trapped behind a Carlos Sainz–Fernando Alonso battle (Sainz got a five-second penalty for ignoring blue flags and drifting into Piastri, who raged over team radio), was overcut by Norris in the pits, then retired with a gearbox failure on lap 56. Max Verstappen salvaged second from a difficult weekend; Mercedes' teenager Kimi Antonelli took third after Lewis Hamilton was demoted by a pit-lane speeding penalty.
fields.why: A year ago McLaren were the benchmark and Antonelli a rookie; that a Mercedes driver now leads by two clear wins' worth of points, and McLaren celebrated its first win only in late July, is the clearest sign yet that the 2026 regulation reset genuinely reshuffled the grid rather than merely tweaking it.

fields.display_body: The 2026-27 Swiss Super League - the country's twelve-team top flight - kicked off this weekend, and the two marquee Sunday fixtures both turned on late comebacks. In front of a sold-out St. Gallen, the hosts trailed to a first-half Umeh Emmanuel goal for Zurich before Lukas Goertler equalised from a worked corner (70') and summer signing Andrin Hunziker deflected in the winner four minutes later for a 2-1 St. Gallen victory. It was a pointed result for FCZ's new coach Marcel Koller - the man who led St. Gallen to their last league title 26 years ago - whose reshaped side created the better first-half chances but left empty-handed. In Bern, Young Boys threw away a 2-0 lead against Sion before Samuel Essende's second-half brace rescued a 4-2 win.
fields.why: For most Swiss towns the Super League — not the World Cup that just finished — is the sport that structures the autumn, and the opening weekend already hints at the season's shape: a champion (Thun) nobody expected to defend, a rebuilt Zürich under a returning veteran coach, and a St. Gallen side punching above its weight at home and in Europe.

fields.display_body: The post-Wimbledon lull is a quiet, lower-tier stretch of the calendar, but this week delivered two genuine breakthroughs. Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger won the WTA Prague Open for her first career title on the women's tour, beating Ukraine's Daria Snigur 7-6(3), 6-2 on Sunday. A day earlier, France's Quentin Halys took the ATP Generali Open in Kitzbuehel - his maiden ATP Tour title - edging Alexander Bublik 6-4, 7-6(8-6). Neither event carries ranking weight near the top of the game, and there was no Swiss winner this week.
fields.why: First titles are the tour's leading indicator — they mark which unseeded names are about to start troubling the seeds at the bigger hard-court events (Canada, Cincinnati, then the US Open) over the next month.

fields.display_body: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) — the attention variant introduced in DeepSeek-V2 that squeezes the key-value cache through a shared low-rank bottleneck (a compression step that cuts memory ~81% at inference, the main cost of long context) — is now in production models, but nobody had checked what the bottleneck keeps and what it throws away. Training a small 114M-parameter transformer end to end and probing its internals, the authors find the compressed channel learns an almost pure "content" representation: it retains entity identity (98%) while discarding positional information, which the model reconstructs elsewhere.
fields.why: MLA is one of the load-bearing tricks behind cheap long context, copied into models most people now use, yet it was adopted for its memory savings without anyone knowing what it costs representationally. A clean "it separates content from position, and here's where position goes" is exactly the kind of grounding that lets the next architecture tweak be deliberate rather than superstitious. That the study runs at 114M rather than frontier scale is the honest caveat.

fields.display_body: When labs fine-tune a model with reinforcement learning (RL — training by reward signal rather than by copying examples), the code that generates candidate answers and the code that updates the weights are usually separate engines, and the generator often runs in lower-precision arithmetic to go fast. That mismatch makes the two disagree about what the model actually said, and past a point the training destabilizes. ACRL (Adaptive Control RL) measures the discrepancy live and keeps it inside a safe band; as a side effect it raises policy entropy, nudging the model to keep exploring rather than collapsing onto one answer.
fields.why: RL post-training is now how reasoning models are made, and "our run diverged and we don't know why" is a common and expensive failure. Naming the training-inference gap as a controllable quantity — not an unavoidable artifact of the systems stack — turns a mysterious instability into a dial.

fields.display_body: A reward model is the learned judge that scores answers during alignment training — get it wrong and every model trained against it inherits the bias. Measuring "counterfactual memorization" (how much a specific training pair changed the model versus what it generalized), the authors show reward models misallocate memory to easy, high-margin preference pairs, latch onto dataset-specific shortcuts like which model produced an answer, and over-generalize crude correlates of human preference — longer answers, more compliant tone — when they meet unfamiliar comparisons.
fields.why: "the model is well-aligned" ultimately rests on the reward model judging quality rather than surface features, and this is direct evidence that today's discriminatively-trained judges are not yet doing that in context-dependent cases. It's a caution for anyone treating a reward score as ground truth.

fields.display_body: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) drove much of the recent reasoning-model progress, but it only works where correctness can be checked automatically — arithmetic, unit tests — leaving open-ended writing or dialogue dependent on costly, biased LLM-judges. RLSVR (the "S" for self-verifiable) borrows a trick from self-supervised learning: it transforms an open-ended task into a proxy task the model can grade itself against (for example, reconstructing a corrupted target), manufacturing a verifiable reward from the data rather than an external judge.
fields.why: the biggest limitation on the RLVR recipe is the shrinking supply of tasks with a clean automatic grader. If self-verifiable proxies hold up, that unlocks the same training machinery for the messy majority of tasks where "is this good?" has no unit test — though whether the proxy actually rewards the quality you care about is the thing to scrutinize.

fields.display_body: Recent work shows a tiny amount of poisoned fine-tuning data can install targeted misbehavior, and even innocuous-looking data can transmit hidden preferences. Standard defenses (filtering, mixing in clean data, regularization) dampen but don't remove the effect. This paper pursues robustness through redundancy: fine-tune a separate model on each data source, then at generation time combine their next-token predictions with a consensus rule (e.g. a token-wise minimum), so anything only one poisoned source wanted gets suppressed.
fields.why: as organizations fine-tune on data scraped or bought from many sources, "one bad supplier can backdoor your model" is a real supply-chain risk. Consensus-at-decoding is an appealingly simple mitigation — it needs no trust in any single source — at the cost of running several models.

fields.display_body: The quadratic cost of attention dominates diffusion-based video generation. MXFP4 — a 4-bit floating-point format with a small shared scale per block — promises cheap attention but usually wrecks output quality, because power-of-two scaling clips or underflows values and the softmax normalization introduces rounding error. MXAttention is a post-training method (no retraining, no calibration set) that derives an optimal scaling boundary analytically and quantizes the un-normalized softmax terms before summing them, sidestepping both problems.
fields.why: 4-bit attention is one of the few remaining levers for making video generation affordable to serve, and "data-free" matters because gathering representative calibration data is itself a chore. A method that just works from the model's own numerics lowers the barrier — the open question, as always with aggressive quantization, is whether the quality holds up on content outside the tested set.

fields.display_body: A model serving long context has a bounded working memory (the KV-cache — the stored keys and values it attends back over) and must keep deciding which items to drop. Every deployed method — StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV — commits the instant an item arrives, guessing whether it'll be reused. This paper recasts the decision as estimating a hidden signal ("will this be needed?") and points out the missing middle: fixed-lag smoothing, which waits a bounded number of steps, watches which items a correct near-future prediction actually attended to, and only then commits.
fields.why: the KV-cache is the memory wall of long-context serving, and eviction policies are usually hand-designed heuristics. Casting the whole family as points on one axis — how long you wait before committing — is a genuinely clarifying frame, and it suggests a cheap way to approach the unbeatable offline optimum by measuring rather than guessing.

fields.display_body: Scaling laws tell you how loss falls as you add parameters and compute, but not the prior question: for a fixed task, what is the least capacity that can solve it? Working in a simplified linear-attention model, the paper proves that the intrinsic rank of the token-mixing operation is a tight lower bound — any model below it pays an unavoidable error penalty — that gradient descent recovers this rank, and that the rank can be estimated from the data before you train.
fields.why: most capacity decisions are made by trial, expense, and folklore. A principled "this task needs at least rank r, computable up front" is the kind of theory that, if it transfers from the linear surrogate to real attention (the paper's honest open problem), could tell you how big a model has to be before you spend the GPU-hours.

fields.display_body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy both descended on Washington on Tuesday 28 July to meet President Donald Trump, as a long-stalled Russia-sanctions bill neared a Senate vote and the wars in Iran and Ukraine visibly converged. Both leaders were in the US chiefly for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and hawkish backer of both Israel and Ukraine who died on 11 July; Netanyahu was set to meet Trump with the US–Israel war on Iran topping the agenda, while Zelenskyy pressed for anti-ballistic-missile defences and help producing Patriot systems. The sanctions bill Graham championed would impose 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas — including China and India — and Trump has moved at the last minute to fold sanctions on Iran into the same package. The convergence is concrete: Ukraine attacked an Iranian tanker in the Caspian Sea on Saturday 25 July that it says was ferrying drones and components to Russia, Iran has vowed to retaliate, and Russia said more than 390 Ukrainian drones struck the Moscow region overnight. Trump has said talks with Iran are under way during the current pause in US strikes.
fields.why: two wars 2,500 km apart are being wired together through Washington's sanctions machinery and Iran's arms pipeline to Moscow — treat both leaders' framing as advocacy, since each is seeking Trump's backing.

fields.display_body: South Korea's Kospi stock index collapsed 10.8% on Tuesday 28 July, closing at 6,023.66 — its lowest since April — after a rout in chipmaking shares triggered trading circuit-breakers (automatic pauses meant to halt panic selling). Samsung Electronics sank 13.4% and SK Hynix 14.7%; together the two account for a large share of the Seoul market. The sell-off followed a report in the trade publication The Information that China has begun mass-producing homegrown deep-ultraviolet (DUV) lithography tools — the machines that print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, and a capability Western and Korean firms had assumed China was years from matching — stoking fears that Chinese competition could erode the incumbents' lead. European markets opened slightly higher, suggesting the shock stayed largely regional for now.
fields.why: semiconductors are the backbone of South Korea's export economy, so a one-day drop this steep is a real macroeconomic event — and it signals investors are newly worried that China's chip progress could reset a market the West has dominated.

fields.display_body: Chad announced it will withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Hague-based tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and crimes against humanity, and called on other African Union members to follow. Chad's foreign ministry said the court's record shows "undeniable and egregious selectivity," noting that nine of the ICC's 13 investigations since 2002 have concerned African states and that only one of seven people detained came from outside Africa; the ministry framed the exit as confidence in national and African justice, not an abandonment of victims. That selectivity charge is Chad's own characterisation — the ICC counters that several of its African cases were opened at the request of the states themselves — and it lands as Chad's military leader faces opposition accusations of repression.
fields.why: an African state quitting the ICC and lobbying the AU to do the same feeds a long-running push to weaken the court's reach on the continent, at a moment when its authority is already contested.

fields.display_body: A US appeals court has rejected an investor lawsuit against Switzerland over the wipeout of Credit Suisse's AT1 bonds, the federal finance department (EFD) confirmed on Tuesday 28 July. The judges upheld a lower court's finding that when Switzerland's regulator wrote the bonds to zero it acted as a supervisory authority, not a market participant, and so enjoys state immunity and falls outside US jurisdiction. AT1 bonds ("additional tier 1" — subordinated debt created after the 2008 crisis that is designed to absorb losses and prop up a failing bank) worth about US$17.3 billion were written off when the Swiss state orchestrated UBS's emergency takeover of Credit Suisse in spring 2023. A group of international investors had sued in June 2024 for roughly US$370 million; they can still seek review by the full appeals court or the US Supreme Court, though the EFD says the bar for that is "very high." Separate cases continue elsewhere: Switzerland's own Federal Administrative Court partly overturned the write-down in October 2025 after complaints from some 3,600 investors — a ruling FINMA and UBS have appealed to the Federal Supreme Court — and a group of Japanese investors filed an arbitration claim at the ICSID (a World Bank body that settles investment disputes) in late 2025.
fields.why: the US ruling closes one front in the global legal fight over the most contested piece of the CS rescue, but the decisive battles over whether the write-down stands are still open in Swiss courts and international arbitration.

fields.display_body: A fresh heatwave is rolling into an already parched Switzerland, with SRF Meteo forecasting temperatures of 34-39C at their peak on Thursday 30 July and the hot spell likely to last into the first week of August. The 30C mark was expected to be passed again in the north on Tuesday, widespread 35C from Wednesday 29 July, with the highest readings in northwest Switzerland, the lower Aare valley and around Geneva, plus several "tropical nights" (when temperatures stay above 20C) in cities and by the larger lakes. Forecasters see no substantial cooling or the sustained, widespread rain needed to break the drought before mid-August; open-fire and fireworks bans remain in force across much of the country ahead of the 1 August national holiday (this Saturday), and a field fire near Koblenz (Aargau) spread into woodland on Tuesday.
fields.why: this is the same heat-and-drought spell fuelling the wildfires in France and Spain now reaching Swiss soil, and it means the country's biggest civic holiday will again be marked under near-total fire restrictions.
